facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] A process record is adiabatic exactly when $Q[P]=0$; $W_{\mathrm{on}}>0$ denotes work done on the system ([[def-td-process-and-protocol]]).

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] For every admitted closed record in the stated class, $U(x_P^+)-U(x_P^-)=Q[P]+W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]$ ([[post-td-first-law-energy]]).

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] The adopted entropy is a finite scalar state function with values measured in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ ([[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]).

facts.label: L1
facts.text: [L1] $\log$ is strictly increasing, $\log 1=0$, and $\log(xy)=\log x+\log y$ for positive $x,y$ ([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]).

facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] The ideal-gas equations and entropy difference are exactly those stated in the Example; $R>0$ has units $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and $C_V=3R/2$.

facts.label: A2
facts.text: [A2] The gas is the system inside the declared outer boundary: no matter crosses it, its material constitution is fixed, and its mechanical model supplies a total mass $M>0$ and center-of-mass velocities in the fixed chart of [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. The gas center of mass is at rest at both endpoint preparations, so $\Delta K_{\mathrm{cm}}=0$; no separately tracked external-field potential energy changes (the model may take that term to be absent), so $\Delta U_{\mathrm{ext}}=0$. Thus the admitted record is in $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ as defined by [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. Its protocol has $Q[P]=0$, a constant external load $p_f$ during compression, and $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]=p_f(V_i-V_f)$. The final equilibrium obeys $p_fV_f=nRT_f$, and the initial equilibrium obeys $p_iV_i=nRT_i$. The apparatus is stipulated to dissipatively settle and to have zero entropy change.

steps.text: Put $\lambda:=p_f/p_i$. The equilibrium equations give $T_f/T_i=\lambda(9/10)$. The first-law balance gives $nC_V(T_f-T_i)=p_f(V_i-V_f)$, hence $(3/2)(\lambda(9/10)-1)=\lambda(1/10)$. Solving yields $\lambda=6/5$ and $T_f/T_i=27/25$. [given, F1, F2, A1, A2, algebra]
steps.claim: Put $\lambda:=p_f/p_i$. The equilibrium equations give $T_f/T_i=\lambda(9/10)$. The first-law balance gives $nC_V(T_f-T_i)=p_f(V_i-V_f)$, hence $(3/2)(\lambda(9/10)-1)=\lambda(1/10)$. Solving yields $\lambda=6/5$ and $T_f/T_i=27/25$.

steps.text: The entropy difference is therefore $\Delta S=nR[(3/2)\ln(27/25)+\ln(9/10)]$. By [L1], $2\Delta S/(nR)=\ln\!\left((27/25)^3(9/10)^2\right)=\ln(1594323/1562500)>0$, since $1594323>1562500$ and $\log$ is strictly increasing with $\log 1=0$. Since $nR>0$, $\Delta S>0$. [given, F3, L1, A1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] Each adopted entropy is a finite scalar measured in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ ([[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]).

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] On every specified convex region the entropy is continuous and satisfies the stated Jensen concavity inequality ([[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]).

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] The admitted separated pairs form a designated subset $\mathcal C_{AB}\subseteq D_A\times D_B$ ([[post-td-bulk-additivity]]).

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] Under the composition map, the dimensioned total energy of an admitted pair is $U_{A\sqcup B}=U_A+U_B$ ([[post-td-bulk-additivity]]).

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] For admitted independent separated macroscopic systems, entropy is additive under the composition map ([[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]).

facts.label: F6
facts.text: [F6] The tagged bulk family scales its extensive coordinates by $\lambda>0$, and the entropy postulate assumes $S_{c^{(\lambda)}}(\delta_\lambda x)=\lambda S_c(x)$ ([[post-td-bulk-additivity]], [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]).

facts.label: F7
facts.text: [F7] An equilibrium feasible set may be noncompact and need not contain an entropy maximizer ([[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]).

facts.label: F8
facts.text: [F8] Stable equilibrium in this route requires an attained global maximum on the exact feasible set ([[post-td-entropy-maximum]]).

facts.label: L1
facts.text: [L1] For every real $t$ there is a natural number $n\ge1$ with $t<n$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]).

facts.label: L2
facts.text: [L2] The range of every nonempty finite list of real numbers has a greatest member ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]]).

facts.label: L3
facts.text: [L3] On $\mathbb R^6$, the Euclidean norm is defined by the sum of coordinate squares and induces the usual Euclidean metric ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]).

facts.label: L4
facts.text: [L4] A real number $u$ is the supremum of a set $E\subseteq\mathbb R$ exactly when it is an upper bound of $E$ and $u\le v$ for every upper bound $v$ of $E$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] $D_A=D_B=(0,\infty)^3$ in dimensionless $(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n)$ coordinates, with each full domain designated as an open single-phase chart; $\hat V_A,\hat V_B,\hat n_A,\hat n_B>0$ are fixed; total energy is $1\,\mathrm J$; every pair $\phi(x)$ in $\mathcal F=\{\phi(x):0<x<1\}$ is admitted in $\mathcal C_{AB}$; $s_*=1\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$; and $S_A=2s_*\hat U_A$, $S_B=s_*\hat U_B$, with the same formulas on each tagged scaled copy.

facts.label: A2
facts.text: [A2] Compactness uses the inherited Euclidean topology: every cover of $\mathcal F$ by relatively open subsets must have a finite subcover.

steps.text: Each entropy in [A1] is finite, affine and continuous on the convex domain $(0,\infty)^3$, hence concave; it is $C^2$ with $S_{A,U}=2\,\mathrm{K^{-1}}$ and $S_{B,U}=1\,\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. Scaling every extensive coordinate by $\lambda$ scales each entropy by $\lambda$, and the admitted separated-system total is their sum. The pairs in [A1] are admitted by [F3], their fixed total energy uses the composition rule [F4], the separated entropy is the sum by [F5], and the tagged scaling is homogeneous by [F6]. Thus the model satisfies [F1]–[F6]. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

steps.text: For each integer $n\ge2$, put $\mathcal U_n=\{\phi(x)\in\mathcal F:x<1-1/n\}$. It is relatively open: if $\phi(x)\in\mathcal U_n$, then $\epsilon=1-1/n-x>0$, and any $\phi(y)\in\mathcal F$ with $\|\phi(y)-\phi(x)\|_2<\epsilon$ has coordinate difference $\phi(y)-\phi(x)=(y-x,0,0,-(y-x),0,0)$. By [L3], $\|\phi(y)-\phi(x)\|_2=\sqrt2|y-x|$, so $|y-x|<\epsilon$ and $y<1-1/n$. Given any $x\in(0,1)$, [L1] applied to $1/(1-x)>1$ gives an integer $n>1/(1-x)$; then $n\ge2$ and $x<1-1/n$, so the $\mathcal U_n$ cover $\mathcal F$. For any nonempty finite subfamily with indices $n_1,\ldots,n_k$, [L2] gives a greatest index $N$, and its union is $\mathcal U_N$. The feasible state $\phi(1-1/(2N))$ belongs to $\mathcal F$ but not $\mathcal U_N$, so this cover has no finite subcover. By [A2] and [F7], $\mathcal F$ is noncompact and has no assumed attainment guarantee. [given, A1, A2, F7, L1, L2, L3, algebra]

steps.text: For every $x\in(0,1)$, the entropy value is $S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\phi(x))=s_*(1+x)<2s_*$ because $s_*>0$. Thus $2s_*$ is an upper bound of the feasible entropy values. [given, A1, step 1.1, algebra]
steps.claim: For every $x\in(0,1)$, the entropy value is $S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\phi(x))=s_*(1+x)<2s_*$ because $s_*>0$. Thus $2s_*$ is an upper bound of the feasible entropy values.

steps.text: Given any $\varepsilon>0$, apply [L1] to $2+s_*/\varepsilon$ to choose $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n>2+s_*/\varepsilon$. Then $x_n:=1-1/n\in(0,1)$ and $$0<2s_*-S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\phi(x_n))=s_*/n<\varepsilon.$$ Hence feasible entropy values lie arbitrarily close to $2s_*$ from below. [given, A1, L1, step 1.1, algebra]
steps.claim: Given any $\varepsilon>0$, apply [L1] to $2+s_*/\varepsilon$ to choose $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n>2+s_*/\varepsilon$. Then $x_n:=1-1/n\in(0,1)$ and $$0<2s_*-S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\phi(x_n))=s_*/n<\varepsilon.$$ Hence feasible entropy values lie arbitrarily close to $2s_*$ from below.

steps.text: Let $u$ be any upper bound of the feasible entropy values. If $u<2s_*$, set $d:=2s_*-u>0$ and apply [L1] to $2+s_*/d$ to choose $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n>2+s_*/d$. Then $x:=1-1/n\in(0,1)$ and $S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\phi(x))=2s_*-s_*/n>2s_*-d=u$, contradicting that $u$ is an upper bound. Therefore $2s_*\le u$ for every upper bound $u$. By [L4], $\sup\{S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\phi(x)):0<x<1\}=2s_*$. [given, A1, L1, L4, step 1.1, algebra]
steps.claim: Let $u$ be any upper bound of the feasible entropy values. If $u<2s_*$, set $d:=2s_*-u>0$ and apply [L1] to $2+s_*/d$ to choose $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n>2+s_*/d$. Then $x:=1-1/n\in(0,1)$ and $S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\phi(x))=2s_*-s_*/n>2s_*-d=u$, contradicting that $u$ is an upper bound. Therefore $2s_*\le u$ for every upper bound $u$. By [L4], $\sup\{S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\phi(x)):0<x<1\}=2s_*$.

steps.text: For every $x\in(0,1)$, $y=(x+1)/2$ also lies in $(0,1)$ and satisfies $y>x$. Hence $S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\phi(y))=s_*(1+y)>s_*(1+x)=S_{\mathrm{tot}}(\phi(x))$ because $s_*>0$. No feasible state maximizes entropy; the supremum $2s_*$ is not attained because $x=1$ is excluded. [given, A1, step 1.1, algebra]

steps.text: By [F8] stable equilibrium in this route requires an attained global maximum on the exact feasible set. Since no maximum is attained, this model has no stable equilibrium under that criterion. [F8, step 2.4] ∎

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[def-complete-ordered-field]]: every nonempty subset of an ordered field that is bounded above has a least upper bound.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[def-natural-numbers]], [[def-nat-addition]], [[lem-nat-add-commutative]], [[lem-nat-add-identity]], and [[def-nat-order]]: $\mathbb N$ is the von Neumann set of naturals, its successor is $\sigma(n)=n+1$, and $m\le n$ means $m+k=n$ for some $k\in\mathbb N$. Since $1+n=n+1=\sigma(n)$, every successor is at least $1$. Natural indices remain in $\mathbb N$; in field expressions the successor is carried into $\mathbb R$ by the canonical natural map of [[def-canonical-natural]].

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[def-canonical-natural]] and [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]: write $\iota_{\mathbb N}:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical natural map, with $\iota_{\mathbb N}(0)=0$ and $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))=\iota_{\mathbb N}(n)+1$. It is positive on positive naturals and strictly increases there. Thus the displayed denominator $n+1$ means $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))$, not a von Neumann set used as a real number.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[lem-of-q-embeds]]: the rational embedding into $\mathbb R$ preserves order, so every rational $q>0$ has positive real image $\hat q$. [[cor-of-one-positive]], [[lem-of-inverse-positive]], and [[lem-of-sign-rules]] supply $1>0$, positivity of the inverse of a positive real, and reversal of order by reciprocation on positive reals.

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[def-real-limit]]: a real sequence converges to $0$ when, for every rational $q>0$, its absolute value is eventually less than $\hat q$.

steps.text: The set $N_{\mathbb R}:=\{\iota_{\mathbb N}(n):n\in\mathbb N\}$ is nonempty. If it were bounded above, completeness [F1] would give $s=\sup N_{\mathbb R}$. Since $1>0$ by [F4], $s-1<s$, so $s-1$ is not an upper bound; choose $n\in\mathbb N$ with $\iota_{\mathbb N}(n)>s-1$. By the successor rule in [F3], $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))=\iota_{\mathbb N}(n)+1>s$, while $\sigma(n)\in\mathbb N$, contradicting that $s$ is an upper bound. Hence $N_{\mathbb R}$ is unbounded above. [F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]
steps.claim: The set $N_{\mathbb R}:=\{\iota_{\mathbb N}(n):n\in\mathbb N\}$ is nonempty. If it were bounded above, completeness [F1] would give $s=\sup N_{\mathbb R}$. Since $1>0$ by [F4], $s-1<s$, so $s-1$ is not an upper bound; choose $n\in\mathbb N$ with $\iota_{\mathbb N}(n)>s-1$. By the successor rule in [F3], $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))=\iota_{\mathbb N}(n)+1>s$, while $\sigma(n)\in\mathbb N$, contradicting that $s$ is an upper bound. Hence $N_{\mathbb R}$ is unbounded above.

steps.text: For every $n\in\mathbb N$, $\sigma(n)=1+n$ by natural-addition commutativity and the successor rule, so $1\le\sigma(n)$ by the definition of natural order; hence $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))>0$ by [F3]. The successor recursion gives $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(\sigma(n)))=\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))+1>\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))$, since $1>0$. Reciprocation reverses this strict inequality by [F4], hence $0<\epsilon_n$ and $\epsilon_{n+1}<\epsilon_n$. Now fix rational $q>0$ and let $\hat q>0$ be its real image. By step 1.1 choose $N\in\mathbb N$ with $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(N))>1/\hat q$. If $n\ge N$, then $\sigma(N)\le\sigma(n)$ by [F2] and [[lem-nat-order-add-compatible]], and the increasing-map clause of [F3] gives $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))\ge\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(N))$. Therefore $0<\epsilon_n\le 1/\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(N))<\hat q$. This is convergence to zero by [F5]. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

The successor recursion gives $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(\sigma(n)))=\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))+1>\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))$, since $1>0$. Reciprocation reverses this strict inequality by [F4], hence $0<\epsilon_n$ and $\epsilon_{n+1}<\epsilon_n$. Now fix rational $q>0$ and let $\hat q>0$ be its real image. If $n\ge N$, then $\sigma(N)\le\sigma(n)$ by [F2] and [[lem-nat-order-add-compatible]], and the increasing-map clause of [F3] gives $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))\ge\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(N))$. Therefore $0<\epsilon_n\le 1/\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(N))<\hat q$. This is convergence to zero by [F5].

facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]]: equal-mass compounds form a preorder with consistency, positive scaling, stability for fixed positive spectators, and CH.

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]]: $e_x$ has mass one, compound masses are finite sums, and composition/scaling preserve the stated masses.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]] and [[lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation]]: signed comparisons are well-defined, translation-invariant, and agree with ordinary comparison on nonnegative compounds. For a finite-support signed map $u$, write $u^+(y):=\max\{u(y),0\}$ and $u^-(y):=\max\{-u(y),0\}$ pointwise; these are finite-support nonnegative maps with $u+u^-=u^+$, and this notation extends the positive and negative parts used in [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]] to each signed reference map $R_\lambda$ itself.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[lem-tdmath-reference-order]]: $R_\lambda\preceq_sR_\mu$ exactly when $\lambda\le\mu$.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[lem-tdmath-reciprocal-naturals-tend-zero]]: for $n\in\mathbb N$, $\epsilon_n:=1/q_n$ with $q_n:=\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))$ is positive, strictly decreasing, and converges to zero. Its canonical-natural convention gives $\iota_{\mathbb N}(n)\ge0$ and $q_n=\iota_{\mathbb N}(n)+1\ge1$; natural indices and their real images are distinguished.

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[def-complete-ordered-field]]: every nonempty bounded-above subset of $\mathbb R$ has a supremum.

steps.text: Write $q_n:=\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))>0$, so $\epsilon_n=1/q_n$ by [F4]. Suppose no $n\in\mathbb N$ satisfies $(q_n+1)e_{x_0}\preceq q_ne_{x_1}+e_x$. Both sides have mass $q_n+1$, so CH gives $q_ne_{x_1}+e_x\preceq(q_n+1)e_{x_0}$. Scale by $1/q_n=\epsilon_n$ to obtain $e_{x_1}+\epsilon_ne_x\preceq e_{x_0}+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}$. Apply stability to the sequence $\epsilon_n$, with bases $e_{x_1},e_{x_0}$ and positive unit-mass spectators $e_x,e_{x_0}$. It yields $x_1\preceq x_0$, contradicting strictness. Thus some $n$ has $(q_n+1)e_{x_0}\preceq q_ne_{x_1}+e_x$, which by signed translation and cancellation in [F2] is $R_{-q_n}\preceq_s e_x$; hence $-q_n\in L_x$. [A1, F1, F2, F4]

Both sides have mass $q_n+1$, so CH gives $q_ne_{x_1}+e_x\preceq(q_n+1)e_{x_0}$. Scale by $1/q_n=\epsilon_n$ to obtain $e_{x_1}+\epsilon_ne_x\preceq e_{x_0}+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}$. Apply stability to the sequence $\epsilon_n$, with bases $e_{x_1},e_{x_0}$ and positive unit-mass spectators $e_x,e_{x_0}$. It yields $x_1\preceq x_0$, contradicting strictness. Thus some $n$ has $(q_n+1)e_{x_0}\preceq q_ne_{x_1}+e_x$, which by signed translation and cancellation in [F2] is $R_{-q_n}\preceq_s e_x$; hence $-q_n\in L_x$.

steps.text: Suppose $L_x$ is unbounded above. For each $n\in\mathbb N$, unboundedness supplies $\lambda\in L_x$ with $\lambda>q_n$; [F3] gives $R_{q_n}\preceq_sR_\lambda$, and transitivity gives $q_n\in L_x$. Since $q_n\ge1$ by [F4], adding the common compound $q_ne_{x_0}$ to $R_{q_n}$ and $e_x$ makes them $e_{x_0}+q_ne_{x_1}$ and $e_x+q_ne_{x_0}$. Thus [F2] identifies $R_{q_n}\preceq_s e_x$ with the compound comparison between those maps. Scaling by $\epsilon_n=1/q_n$ gives $e_{x_1}+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}\preceq e_{x_0}+\epsilon_ne_x$. Stability with bases $e_{x_1},e_{x_0}$ and positive unit-mass spectators $e_{x_0},e_x$ now yields $x_1\preceq x_0$, again a contradiction. Therefore $L_x$ is bounded above. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4]
steps.claim: Suppose $L_x$ is unbounded above. For each $n\in\mathbb N$, unboundedness supplies $\lambda\in L_x$ with $\lambda>q_n$; [F3] gives $R_{q_n}\preceq_sR_\lambda$, and transitivity gives $q_n\in L_x$. Since $q_n\ge1$ by [F4], adding the common compound $q_ne_{x_0}$ to $R_{q_n}$ and $e_x$ makes them $e_{x_0}+q_ne_{x_1}$ and $e_x+q_ne_{x_0}$. Thus [F2] identifies $R_{q_n}\preceq_s e_x$ with the compound comparison between those maps. Scaling by $\epsilon_n=1/q_n$ gives $e_{x_1}+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}\preceq e_{x_0}+\epsilon_ne_x$. Stability with bases $e_{x_1},e_{x_0}$ and positive unit-mass spectators $e_{x_0},e_x$ now yields $x_1\preceq x_0$, again a contradiction. Therefore $L_x$ is bounded above.

steps.text: If $\lambda\in L_x$ and $\mu\le\lambda$, [F3] gives $R_\mu\preceq_sR_\lambda$; signed transitivity and $R_\lambda\preceq_s e_x$ imply $\mu\in L_x$. Thus $L_x$ is downward closed. By steps 1.1 and 1.2 it is nonempty and bounded above, so [F5] supplies the real number $s:=\sup L_x$. [A1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2]
steps.claim: If $\lambda\in L_x$ and $\mu\le\lambda$, [F3] gives $R_\mu\preceq_sR_\lambda$; signed transitivity and $R_\lambda\preceq_s e_x$ imply $\mu\in L_x$. Thus $L_x$ is downward closed. By steps 1.1 and 1.2 it is nonempty and bounded above, so [F5] supplies the real number $s:=\sup L_x$.

steps.text: For each $n\in\mathbb N$, $s-\epsilon_n$ is not an upper bound of $L_x$, so some $\lambda\in L_x$ has $\lambda>s-\epsilon_n$. Downward closure gives $s-\epsilon_n\in L_x$. Consistency then gives $R_s+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}\preceq_s e_x+\epsilon_ne_{x_1}$, because $R_{s-\epsilon_n}+\epsilon_ne_{x_1}=R_s+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}$. Let $K:=R_s^-$. Adding the fixed nonnegative map $K$ to both sides converts this signed comparison into the compound comparison $R_s^++\epsilon_ne_{x_0}\preceq e_x+K+\epsilon_ne_{x_1}$. Their bases have equal mass because $m(R_s^+)-m(K)=1=m(e_x)$. Stability with positive unit-mass spectators $e_{x_0},e_{x_1}$ yields $R_s^+\preceq e_x+K$, that is, $R_s\preceq_s e_x$. [A1, F1, F2, F4, step 2.1]
steps.claim: For each $n\in\mathbb N$, $s-\epsilon_n$ is not an upper bound of $L_x$, so some $\lambda\in L_x$ has $\lambda>s-\epsilon_n$. Downward closure gives $s-\epsilon_n\in L_x$. Consistency then gives $R_s+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}\preceq_s e_x+\epsilon_ne_{x_1}$, because $R_{s-\epsilon_n}+\epsilon_ne_{x_1}=R_s+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}$. Let $K:=R_s^-$. Adding the fixed nonnegative map $K$ to both sides converts this signed comparison into the compound comparison $R_s^++\epsilon_ne_{x_0}\preceq e_x+K+\epsilon_ne_{x_1}$. Their bases have equal mass because $m(R_s^+)-m(K)=1=m(e_x)$. Stability with positive unit-mass spectators $e_{x_0},e_{x_1}$ yields $R_s^+\preceq e_x+K$, that is, $R_s\preceq_s e_x$.

steps.text: Since $s$ is an upper bound, $s+\epsilon_n\notin L_x$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$. To derive the reverse signed comparison from CH, set $H_n:=R_{s+\epsilon_n}^-$. The translated maps $e_x+H_n$ and $R_{s+\epsilon_n}+H_n=R_{s+\epsilon_n}^+$ are nonnegative compounds. Since $R_{s+\epsilon_n}=R_{s+\epsilon_n}^+-H_n$ has total coefficient one, finite-sum linearity gives $m(R_{s+\epsilon_n}^+)-m(H_n)=1$; with $m(e_x)=1$, the translated compounds have equal mass $1+m(H_n)$. CH applies to this pair. If it gave $R_{s+\epsilon_n}^+\preceq e_x+H_n$, signed translation invariance in [F2] would imply $R_{s+\epsilon_n}\preceq_s e_x$, contrary to $s+\epsilon_n\notin L_x$. Therefore it gives $e_x+H_n\preceq R_{s+\epsilon_n}^+$, which by [F2] is $e_x\preceq_s R_{s+\epsilon_n}$. Add $\epsilon_ne_{x_0}$ to both signed maps and use $R_{s+\epsilon_n}+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}=R_s+\epsilon_ne_{x_1}$. Then add $K=R_s^-$ to both; the resulting equal-mass compound comparison is $e_x+K+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}\preceq R_s^++\epsilon_ne_{x_1}$. Stability with bases $e_x+K,R_s^+$ and positive unit-mass spectators $e_{x_0},e_{x_1}$ gives $e_x+K\preceq R_s^+$, or $e_x\preceq_sR_s$. Together with step 3.1 this proves $R_s\sim_s e_x$ and the claimed attainment. [A1, F1, F2, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] The finite row data in the Statement: $m,n$ are nonnegative integers, and each row is $(c_j,h_j)$ with real coefficients.

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[def-complete-ordered-field]] supplies the complete ordered real field; [[def-function-space]] defines $\mathbb R^n$ as functions on $n=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ with pointwise coordinate operations, forming a vector space as in [[def-vector-space]], including the one-element zero space when $n=0$. The dot product and finite vector sums are exactly those defined in the Statement.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[def-finite-sum]] and clauses 1 and 2 of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] supply finite-sum additivity and scalar linearity. [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]] supplies finite-set enumeration, bijective reindexing and interchange of finite iterated sums; applied to $\mathbb R$ and its pointwise function spaces, these laws justify collecting coordinates and coefficients in finite row combinations.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[lem-of-sign-rules]]: a product of positive reals is positive, multiplying an inequality by a positive real preserves its direction, and multiplication by zero yields equality.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[thm-induction-principle]]: a property of the natural-number length that holds at zero and passes from each length to its successor holds at every finite length.

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]: each nonzero natural number $n$ has a predecessor $n'$ with $n=\sigma(n')$.

steps.text: If $b$ solves the system and $\lambda_j\ge0$ with $\sum_j\lambda_jc_j=0$, multiply row $j$ by $\lambda_j$ and add the finitely many inequalities. By [F3] each row inequality is preserved under its nonnegative multiplier. By the coordinatewise definitions in the Statement and finite-sum distributivity with Fubini from [F2], $\sum_{j<m}\lambda_j(c_j\cdot b)=(\sum_{j<m}\lambda_jc_j)\cdot b=0$. Hence $0\ge\sum_{j<m}\lambda_jh_j$. This proves necessity. [A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

steps.text: For sufficiency, prove by induction on $n$ the alternative: if the finite system has no solution, there is a nonnegative combination of its rows whose coefficient vector is zero and whose right side is positive. If $n=0$, every row has zero left side; infeasibility means some $h_j>0$, and that single row is the certificate. If $m=0$, the system is feasible, so this case cannot occur under the induction claim's antecedent. [A1, F1, F4]

If $n=0$, every row has zero left side; infeasibility means some $h_j>0$, and that single row is the certificate. If $m=0$, the system is feasible, so this case cannot occur under the induction claim's antecedent.

steps.text: Let $n>0$ and assume the alternative for $n'$ variables, where $n=\sigma(n')=n'\cup\{n'\}$ by [F5] and [[def-natural-numbers]]. For $c\in\mathbb R^n$ define $a\in\mathbb R^{n'}$ by $a(k):=c(k)$ for $k<n'$, and put $\alpha:=c(n')\in\mathbb R$; this separates its first $n'$ coordinates and its last coordinate. Conversely, each $u\in\mathbb R^{n'}$ and $t\in\mathbb R$ determine the unique $b\in\mathbb R^n$ with $b(k)=u(k)$ for $k<n'$ and $b(n')=t$. For every row $c_j$, define $a_j(k):=c_j(k)$ for $k<n'$ and $\alpha_j:=c_j(n')$. Partition the row indices into $P=\{j:\alpha_j>0\}$, $N=\{j:\alpha_j<0\}$, and $Z=\{j:\alpha_j=0\}$. Retain each row $(a_j,h_j)$ for $j\in Z$. For every $p\in P$ and $q\in N$, add the reduced row $((-\alpha_q)a_p+\alpha_p a_q,\;(-\alpha_q)h_p+\alpha_p h_q)$. Every multiplier used is positive, so these row combinations preserve the inequality directions by [F3]. [A1, F1, F3, F5, algebra]

For $c\in\mathbb R^n$ define $a\in\mathbb R^{n'}$ by $a(k):=c(k)$ for $k<n'$, and put $\alpha:=c(n')\in\mathbb R$; this separates its first $n'$ coordinates and its last coordinate. Conversely, each $u\in\mathbb R^{n'}$ and $t\in\mathbb R$ determine the unique $b\in\mathbb R^n$ with $b(k)=u(k)$ for $k<n'$ and $b(n')=t$. For every row $c_j$, define $a_j(k):=c_j(k)$ for $k<n'$ and $\alpha_j:=c_j(n')$. Partition the row indices into $P=\{j:\alpha_j>0\}$, $N=\{j:\alpha_j<0\}$, and $Z=\{j:\alpha_j=0\}$. Retain each row $(a_j,h_j)$ for $j\in Z$. For every $p\in P$ and $q\in N$, add the reduced row $((-\alpha_q)a_p+\alpha_p a_q,\;(-\alpha_q)h_p+\alpha_p h_q)$. Every multiplier used is positive, so these row combinations preserve the inequality directions by [F3].

steps.text: The reduced system in $u\in\mathbb R^{n'}$ is feasible exactly when the original is, using the coordinate reconstruction in step 1.3. Indeed, a solution $(u,t)$ implies every retained inequality; adding row $p$ multiplied by $-\alpha_q>0$ to row $q$ multiplied by $\alpha_p>0$ cancels $t$ and gives each pair row. Conversely, if $u$ satisfies the reduced system, rows in $P$ impose finitely many lower bounds $t\ge L_p:=(h_p-a_p\cdot u)/\alpha_p$, and rows in $N$ impose finitely many upper bounds $t\le U_q:=(h_q-a_q\cdot u)/\alpha_q$. Each pair row is exactly $L_p\le U_q$. To justify the finite extrema, enumerate any nonempty finite list $\ell_0,\ldots,\ell_{k-1}$ of lower bounds and define $M_1=\ell_0$; for $1\le j<k$, recursively set $M_{j+1}=M_j$ if $M_j\ge\ell_j$, and $M_{j+1}=\ell_j$ otherwise. Totality of the real order makes $M_{j+1}$ the larger of $M_j$ and $\ell_j$; induction [F4] shows that $M_k$ is a member of the list and dominates every entry. Thus a finite nonempty list has a maximum. For an upper-bound list $v_0,\ldots,v_{\ell-1}$, define $m_1=v_0$ and, for $1\le j<\ell$, set $m_{j+1}=m_j$ if $m_j\le v_j$, and $m_{j+1}=v_j$ otherwise. The same totality and induction argument shows $m_\ell$ is a member no greater than any entry, so every finite nonempty list has a minimum. If both $P,N$ are nonempty, these extrema and all pair inequalities give $\max_{p\in P}L_p\le\min_{q\in N}U_q$, so choose $t=\max_{p\in P}L_p$. If only lower bounds occur choose their finite maximum; if only upper bounds occur choose their finite minimum; if neither occurs choose $t=0$. Thus the original system has a solution. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

steps.text: If the original system is infeasible, step 2.1 makes the reduced system infeasible. By induction there are nonnegative multipliers on reduced rows with zero combined first $n'$ coordinates and positive combined right side. Lift each retained zero-row multiplier to its original row; lift each pair-row multiplier $\mu_{pq}$ to coefficients $-\alpha_q\mu_{pq}$ on row $p$ and $\alpha_p\mu_{pq}$ on row $q$. All lifted coefficients are nonnegative by [F3]. Every pair lift has last coordinate $(-\alpha_q)\alpha_p+\alpha_p\alpha_q=0$; the total first coordinates vanish by the reduced certificate, and its right side remains positive. This is the required certificate for the original system and completes the induction. [A1, F3, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra]

steps.text: If the stated multiplier condition holds, the certificate from step 3.1 cannot exist, because it would have zero combined left coefficient and positive combined right side. Therefore the system is feasible. Together with step 1.1 this proves both directions, including the empty-variable base case in step 1.2, the zero/positive/negative sign partition and bound reconstruction in steps 1.3–2.1, and the lifted certificate in step 3.1. [A1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: adopt the Axiom of Choice for the Hahn–Banach and basis-extension steps.

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[def-vector-space]] and [[def-linear-subspace]]: $V$ is a real vector space, and a subset closed under addition and all scalar multiples is a linear subspace.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[def-sublinear-functional]]: a real-valued sublinear functional is positively homogeneous and subadditive.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[thm-hahn-banach-dominated-extension]]: for real vector spaces, a subspace, a real-valued sublinear functional and a linear functional dominated on that subspace, there is a dominated linear extension to the whole space.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[def-complete-ordered-field]]: the real field used in the one-step dominated-extension argument has the least-upper-bound property.

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[cor-every-vector-space-has-a-basis]] and [[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]]: under the adopted choice strength, a vector space has a basis and an independent subset extends to a basis of the ambient space.

facts.label: F6
facts.text: [F6] [[def-linear-independence]] and [[def-linear-basis]]: a basis is an independent spanning set; spanning gives a finite expression for each vector, and independence makes its finite coefficient map unique.

facts.label: F7
facts.text: [F7] [[def-tdmath-type-offset-vector-space]] and [[lem-tdmath-type-offset-vector-space-well-defined]]: the quotient is a real vector space with the declared product and positive-scaling relations.

facts.label: F8
facts.text: [F8] [[def-extended-reals]]: the order and negation on $\mathbb R\cup\{\pm\infty\}$ are extended as defined there; for values in $\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, addition is the real sum when both are real and is $+\infty$ when either is $+\infty$, while multiplication by $t>0$ sends $+\infty$ to $+\infty$. These cases avoid the undefined extended-real operations listed in that definition.

facts.label: F9
facts.text: [F9] [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]: a real-linear functional $L:V\to\mathbb R$ is a linear map, so $L(x+y)=L(x)+L(y)$ and $L(tx)=tL(x)$ for $x,y\in V$ and $t\in\mathbb R$.

facts.label: F10
facts.text: [F10] [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]: since $p$ is a function on the set $V$ and $+\infty$ is in the extended-real codomain, Separation forms the subset $W=\{x\in V:p(x)<+\infty\}$ as a set.

steps.text: By [F10], $W$ is a set. It contains $0$ because $p(0)=0$. If $x,y\in W$, subadditivity gives $p(x+y)\le p(x)+p(y)<+\infty$, so $x+y\in W$ by the extended-real conventions in [F8]. For $t>0$, homogeneity gives $p(tx)=tp(x)<+\infty$. If $t<0$, put $s:=-t>0$; no-sinks gives $-x\in W$, and positive homogeneity applied to $s(-x)=tx$ puts $tx$ in $W$. Also $0x=0\in W$. Thus $W$ is a linear subspace. The restriction $p|_W$ is finite-valued, positively homogeneous and subadditive, so it is a real-valued sublinear functional. [F1, F2, F8, F10, algebra]

For $t>0$, homogeneity gives $p(tx)=tp(x)<+\infty$. If $t<0$, put $s:=-t>0$; no-sinks gives $-x\in W$, and positive homogeneity applied to $s(-x)=tx$ puts $tx$ in $W$. Also $0x=0\in W$. Thus $W$ is a linear subspace. The restriction $p|_W$ is finite-valued, positively homogeneous and subadditive, so it is a real-valued sublinear functional.

steps.text: Let $M=\{0\}\subseteq W$ and let $f_0(0)=0$. This is linear and satisfies $f_0(0)=0=p(0)$. The real ordered field is complete by [F4], as used in the one-step interval argument of the published theorem. Apply [F3] to $p|_W$ and $f_0$; it gives a linear $\ell:W\to\mathbb R$ with $\ell(x)\le p(x)$ for every $x\in W$. Applying this at $-x\in W$ yields $-\ell(x)=\ell(-x)\le p(-x)$, so $-p(-x)\le\ell(x)\le p(x)$ on $W$. [A1, F3, F4, F8, F9, step 1.1]

Applying this at $-x\in W$ yields $-\ell(x)=\ell(-x)\le p(-x)$, so $-p(-x)\le\ell(x)\le p(x)$ on $W$.

steps.text: By [F5], choose a basis $B_W$ of $W$ and extend its independent set to a basis $B_V$ of $V$. Assign value $\ell(b)$ to $b\in B_W$ and $0$ to $b\in B_V\setminus B_W$. For any $v\in V$, [F6] gives a finite basis expression; define $L(v)$ as the same finite linear combination of assigned real values. If two expressions represented $v$, subtracting and collecting equal basis vectors would give a finite zero combination; independence in [F6] forces every collected coefficient to be zero. Thus $L(v)$ is well-defined. Concatenating finite expressions proves additivity and scalar homogeneity, so $L$ is linear in the sense of [F9]; the basis expression of any $w\in W$ uses only $B_W$, so $L|_W=\ell$. [A1, F5, F6, F9, step 2.1]

steps.text: For $x\in W$, step 3.1 and step 2.1 give $-p(-x)\le L(x)\le p(x)$. facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] The set $\Delta_m$ is nonempty, closed, and bounded: it contains each coordinate vector; it is the intersection of the closed coordinate half-spaces $\{\theta_i\ge0\}$ with the closed affine set $\{\sum_i\theta_i=1\}$; and every coordinate satisfies $0\le\theta_i\le1$, so $\|\theta\|_2^2=\sum_i\theta_i^2\le m$. Hence [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] makes it compact. The map $Q(\theta)=\sum_i\theta_iq_i$ is linear and continuous by [L1], so $\Theta_x=\Delta_m\cap Q^{-1}(\{x\})$ is closed and bounded, hence compact. The objective $\theta\mapsto\sum_i\theta_i a_i$ is also linear and continuous by [L1].

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] A continuous image of a compact metric space is compact ([[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]).

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] A continuous real function on a nonempty compact metric space attains its minimum ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] The epigraph characterizations of extended convexity and lower semicontinuity are [[lem-tdmath-extended-convex-epigraph-equivalence]].

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]: a convex set contains every segment between two of its points.

facts.label: F6
facts.text: [F6] A closed proper convex function equals its biconjugate ([[thm-tdmath-finite-dimensional-biconjugation]]).

facts.label: F7
facts.text: [F7] Equality in Fenchel's inequality is equivalent to the subgradient relation ([[lem-tdmath-fenchel-young-equality]]).

facts.label: L1
facts.text: [L1] [[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]: every linear map between finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces is continuous.

steps.text: The set $\Delta_m$ contains each coordinate vector. The coordinate maps, the sum map $\theta\mapsto\sum_i\theta_i$, and $Q$ are continuous by [L1]. For any continuous map $T$ into a Euclidean space and any closed set $K$, the complement of $T^{-1}(K)$ is open: if $T(z)\notin K$, a ball about $T(z)$ misses $K$, and continuity gives a ball about $z$ mapped inside that ball. Thus $T^{-1}(K)$ is closed. Coordinate half-lines $[0,\infty)$ and singletons are closed, since a point outside either has a positive-distance ball missing it; a finite intersection of closed sets is closed because its complement is a finite union of open sets. These facts show that $\Delta_m$ is closed and that $\Theta_x=\Delta_m\cap Q^{-1}(\{x\})$ is closed. Since $0\le\theta_i\le1$ on $\Delta_m$, both sets are bounded and hence compact by [F1]. For any weights $\theta\in\Delta_m$, prove $h(\sum_i\theta_iq_i)\le\sum_i\theta_i h(q_i)$ by induction on the number $N$ of positive weights: for $N=1$ it is equality; for $N>1$, choose an index $j$ with $0<\theta_j<1$, put $y=(1-\theta_j)^{-1}\sum_{i\ne j}\theta_iq_i$, and apply the induction hypothesis to the normalized remaining weights. steps.text: The set $C+V$ is convex: for $c_1,c_2\in C$, $v_1,v_2\in V$, and $t\in[0,1]$, $(1-t)(c_1+v_1)+t(c_2+v_2)=((1-t)c_1+tc_2)+((1-t)v_1+tv_2)\in C+V$ by [F5]. To see it is closed, fix $z=(x,r)\notin C+V$ and write $c=(u,a)\in C$. The distance from $z$ to the ray $c+V$ is $\rho_z(c)=\sqrt{\|x-u\|_2^2+\max\{a-r,0\}^2}$: if $r\ge a$ the closest ray point has height $r$, and if $r<a$ it has height $a$. This formula is continuous in $c$ because $\max\{w,0\}=(w+|w|)/2$, and it is positive for every $c\in C$ since $z\notin c+V$. Compactness of $C$ and [F3] give a minimum $\delta>0$; every point of $C+V$ is at distance at least $\delta$ from $z$, so the ball of radius $\delta/2$ about $z$ misses $C+V$. steps.text: The species-amount vector is $n(\xi)=n^0+\nu\xi=(2-2\xi,1-\xi,2\xi)^{\mathsf T}$. Nonnegativity of its third component requires $\xi\ge0$, and nonnegativity of its first two components requires $\xi\le1$; hence the feasible set is exactly $[0,1]$. [given, algebra]

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]]: continuous partial derivatives on an open neighborhood imply total differentiability there, with derivative the Jacobian.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[thm-mean-value-inequality-for-total-derivatives]]: on a convex open set, a uniform bound on the derivative operator norm gives the corresponding Lipschitz bound.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: every continuous real component on a compact interval is Riemann integrable.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]: if a continuous function on a closed interval has a Riemann-integrable interior derivative, its integral is the endpoint increment.

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[thm-euclidean-space-complete]]: every Cauchy sequence in $\mathbb R^m$ with its Euclidean norm has a limit in $\mathbb R^m$.

steps.text: By openness choose $R>0$ with $\overline B(q_0,2R)\subset U$. Continuity of $X$ and $DX$ at $q_0$ gives finite $M,L\ge0$ bounding $\|X\|$ on $\overline B(q_0,R)$ and $\|DX\|$ on $B(q_0,2R)$. By [F1] $X$ is totally differentiable there, and [F2] applied to the convex ball $B(q_0,2R)$ gives $\|X(u)-X(v)\|\le L\|u-v\|$ for $u,v\in\overline B(q_0,R)$. [given, F1, F2]

steps.text: Choose $\delta>0$ with $M\delta\le R/2$ and $L\delta<1$, and let $\mathcal C:=\{\gamma\in C([-\delta,\delta],\mathbb R^m):\gamma(t)\in\overline B(q_0,R)\text{ for every }t\}$ with the supremum norm. It is complete: for a supremum-Cauchy sequence $(\gamma_k)$, [F5] gives the pointwise limit $\gamma(t)\in\mathbb R^m$; the supremum-Cauchy estimate, passed to that pointwise limit, gives uniform convergence to $\gamma$. The limit is continuous: given $\varepsilon>0$ and $t_0$, choose $k$ with $\|\gamma_k-\gamma\|_\infty<\varepsilon/3$, then continuity gives $\rho>0$ such that $\|\gamma_k(t)-\gamma_k(t_0)\|<\varepsilon/3$ whenever $|t-t_0|<\rho$; the triangle inequality yields $\|\gamma(t)-\gamma(t_0)\|<\varepsilon$. Also $\gamma(t)\in\overline B(q_0,R)$ for every $t$, since this Euclidean ball is closed and each $\gamma_k(t)$ lies in it. Thus $\gamma\in\mathcal C$. For $p\in\overline B(q_0,R/2)$ define $T_p\gamma(t):=p+\int_0^t X(\gamma(s))\,ds$. The integrand is continuous and hence integrable by [F3]. Then $T_p$ maps $\mathcal C$ into itself, since $\|T_p\gamma(t)-q_0\|\le\|p-q_0\|+M|t|\le R$, and is a contraction with constant at most $L\delta$. [step 1.1, F2, F3, F5, construct]

steps.text: Starting at the constant curve $\gamma_0(t)=p$, iterate $\gamma_{k+1}=T_p\gamma_k$. facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[lem-tdmath-local-contraction-flow]]: a continuous-derivative vector field has a unique local flow, a Volterra integral equation, locally Lipschitz dependence on initial data, and the local flow law.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: for totally differentiable maps, $D(g\circ f)=Dg\circ Df$ at the corresponding point.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]] and [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]: continuous coefficient functions are integrable on compact intervals, and an integrable interior derivative evaluates by its endpoint increment.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] and [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]]: a closed bounded Euclidean ball is compact, and continuous finite-dimensional derivative fields on it are uniformly continuous.

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[thm-euclidean-space-complete]]: every Euclidean Cauchy sequence in a finite-dimensional real coordinate space converges. Consequently, continuous curves into the finite-dimensional matrix and bilinear-map spaces below are complete in the supremum operator norm: a supremum-Cauchy sequence is coordinatewise uniformly Cauchy, its coordinate limits are continuous by uniform convergence, and the bounds $\|A\|_{\rm op}\le\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}|$ and $\|B\|_{\rm op}\le\sum_{k,i,j}|B_{kij}|$ turn coordinatewise uniform convergence into uniform operator-norm convergence.

facts.label: F6
facts.text: [F6] [[thm-banach-fixed-point]]: a contraction from a nonempty complete metric space to itself has a unique fixed point.

facts.label: F7
facts.text: [F7] [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]]: if all first partial derivatives of a map exist on a neighborhood and are continuous at a point, the map is totally differentiable there with the Jacobian as derivative.

steps.text: For $p$ near $q$ put $\Delta_h(t):=\phi_X^t(p+h)-\phi_X^t(p)$. steps.text: Let $\mathcal I=[-\delta,\delta]$ and let $\mathcal C_1=C(\mathcal I,M_m(\mathbb R))$ with the supremum operator norm. facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[def-tdmath-one-form-and-horizontal-path]]: exterior differentiation is coordinate antisymmetrized partial differentiation, and $\wedge$ is the alternating exterior product.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: coordinate compositions with line segments obey the total-derivative chain rule.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]] and [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]: continuous partial derivatives are integrable on coordinate intervals, and their interval integrals give endpoint differences.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] and [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]]: a closed coordinate rectangle is compact and continuous second partials on it are uniformly continuous.

steps.text:
Fix $q\in U$ and distinct coordinates $i,j$. Choose $h,k>0$ small enough that the coordinate rectangle from $q$ to $q+he_i+ke_j$ lies in $U$, and set $\Delta=S(q+he_i+ke_j)-S(q+he_i)-S(q+ke_j)+S(q)$. By [F4] the second partials are uniformly continuous on the chosen closed rectangle. Applying [F2] to coordinate segments and [F3] to their continuous derivatives, Newton–Leibniz gives
$$\Delta=\int_0^h\!\int_0^k S_{ij}(q+se_i+te_j)\,dt\,ds=\int_0^k\!\int_0^h S_{ji}(q+se_i+te_j)\,ds\,dt.$$
Each equality follows by taking the two endpoint differences in the outer coordinate and then applying Newton–Leibniz to the inner difference; both integrands are continuous by $S\in C^2$. [F2, F3, F4]

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[def-tdmath-one-form-and-horizontal-path]]: $\omega_q$ is a covector and $H_q=\ker\omega_q$ is its rank-$n$ horizontal subspace; $d\omega$ and the alternating products are the stated coordinate forms.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[lem-tdmath-local-contraction-flow]]: a $C^1$ vector field has a unique local flow with local inverse and Lipschitz dependence.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[lem-tdmath-variational-flow-and-commutation]]: for $C^2$ fields, local flows are $C^2$ and commute when their bracket vanishes.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[lem-tdmath-exact-multiple-implies-pfaff-integrability]]: $dS=\mu\omega$ with $S\in C^2$ and nowhere-zero $\mu\in C^1$ implies $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$.

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: the derivative of a composition is the composition of derivatives.

facts.text: [L1] [[thm-tdmath-local-implicit-rank]] (the current carrier is `draft`, inventoried on the batch-4 A page, order 268): for $1\le q\le m$, $F:O\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^q$ is $C^1$, $F(x_*)=0$, and some $q\times q$ minor of $DF(x_*)$ is invertible; if $q<m$, after permuting $x=(u,v)\in\mathbb R^{m-q}\times\mathbb R^q$, there are open neighborhoods and a unique $C^1$ graph $v=\varphi(u)$ equivalent to $F(u,v)=0$. Its inspected proof reduces to the published Euclidean implicit-function theorem in the $q<m$ case and to the published inverse-function theorem when $q=m$. In this use $m=2(n+1)$ and $q=n+1<m$, and the solved-coordinate minor is $D\Phi(0)$; the interface matches. The rank carrier's proof contract and dependencies pass scoped checks, but its phase-number precheck reports a canonical-label repair and its Step1 readiness record is missing, so this cross-batch use remains conditional.

steps.text: Since $\omega_{q_0}\ne0$, one coordinate coefficient is nonzero at $q_0$; relabel that coordinate as $z$ and shrink the neighborhood so $b\ne0$. facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[def-tdmath-one-form-and-horizontal-path]]: a horizontal path is piecewise $C^1$, with finitely many pieces, and its tangent lies in $\ker\omega$; constant paths, reversal and finite concatenation are admissible.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[lem-tdmath-local-contraction-flow]] and [[lem-tdmath-variational-flow-and-commutation]]: $C^2$ vector fields have unique local $C^2$ flows, available for both time signs, with inverse flow and differentiable dependence.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] and [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: composition derivatives obey the chain rule, and a real differentiable function with zero derivative on an interval is constant.

facts.label: L1
facts.text: [L1] [[thm-tdmath-local-implicit-rank]]: a $C^1$ zero equation with a specified invertible solved-coordinate minor has a local $C^1$ graph. The batch-4 draft carrier and its proof have been inspected; deductions using it remain conditional on that supplier's final acceptance.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[thm-connected-subsets-of-r-are-intervals]]: every interval is connected; it cannot be partitioned into two nonempty relatively open sets.

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[thm-rationals-countable]] and [[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]]: the rational numbers admit an enumeration and are dense in the reals, without a choice hypothesis. Finite words and finite rational tuples can be enumerated by length and by the sum of their integer indices.

facts.label: F6
facts.text: [F6] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]] and [[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]: a closed bounded parameter box is compact; its continuous image is compact and closed in the Euclidean ambient space. These suppliers are choice-free.

facts.label: F7
facts.text: [F7] [[thm-euclidean-space-complete]]: every Euclidean Cauchy sequence converges, coordinatewise from real completeness.

facts.label: F8
facts.text: [F8] [[thm-recursion]] and [[thm-well-ordering-principle]]: a recursively prescribed least natural-number index defines a sequence without arbitrary selections.

steps.text: Use the local first integrals in the Statement. Write $\omega=\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}\omega_j dx_j$ in the fixed Euclidean coordinates and set $w=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_{n+1})$ and $Z_j=e_j-(\omega_j/|w|^2)w$. These globally defined $C^2$ vector fields are horizontal and span $\ker\omega$ at each point, since their matrix is the orthogonal projection onto that kernel. On every neighborhood supplied by the hypothesis, $dS=\mu\omega$ has nonzero derivative, and each $Z_j$-flow preserves $S$ as long as its trajectory remains there, by [F3]. Its derivative therefore preserves horizontal tangent vectors there: differentiating $S(\phi_j^t(x))=S(x)$ gives $dS_{\phi_j^t(x)}D\phi_j^t(x)v=dS_xv=0$ for horizontal $v$. The compact image of any finite flow trajectory has a finite subcover by such neighborhoods; a sufficiently fine finite subdivision of its compact time interval puts each subtrajectory in one of them. This follows directly from compactness: otherwise shrinking subintervals failing the subdivision would have a limiting time whose neighborhood contains them. Composing the local derivative identities obtains preservation over the full duration. Local flow uniqueness makes these continuations consistent, and [F2] gives $C^2$ dependence on durations and initial points wherever the finite composition is defined. steps.text: Fix $q\in U$ and a neighborhood $W$ with $dS=\mu\omega$ as in the hypothesis. Since $dS_q=\mu(q)\omega_q\ne0$, apply [L1] to $x\mapsto S(x)-S(q)$ with ambient dimension $n+1$ and target dimension $1$; after choosing the solved coordinate, its zero set is a local $C^1$ graph plaque $P$ through $q$, parameterized by its $n$ free coordinates. Let $\pi$ be projection to those free coordinates. Choose $n$ of the fields $Z_j$ that form a basis of $\ker\omega_q=\ker dS_q$, and for $s=(s_1,\ldots,s_n)$ near $0$ let $E(s)$ be the endpoint at $q$ of the successive local flows of these fields for durations $s_1,\ldots,s_n$. Shrink the open duration domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ so all flow segments stay in $W$. Step 1.1 shows that each flow preserves $S$, so $E(D)\subseteq P$; moreover $DE(0)$ has the chosen basis as its columns. The differential $D(\pi\circ E)(0)$ is therefore an invertible $n\times n$ matrix, because $D\pi_q$ is an isomorphism from the tangent space of the graph plaque to its free-coordinate space. Choose an open neighborhood $Y\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $y_0=\pi(q)$ and shrink $D$ so that the target-augmented map $H:D\times Y\to\mathbb R^n$, $H(s,y):=\pi(E(s))-y$, is defined. It satisfies $H(0,y_0)=0$ and its solved block $D_sH(0,y_0)=D(\pi\circ E)(0)$ is invertible. Apply [L1] with ambient dimension $2n$ and target dimension $n<2n$, permuting inputs to $(y,s)$ so $y$ is free and $s$ is solved. For every $y$ near $y_0$ this gives $s(y)$ with $\pi(E(s(y)))=y$; uniqueness of the graph plaque then says the endpoints $E(s(y))$ fill a relative neighborhood of $q$ in $P$. Each is reachable by a finite word of horizontal flows inside $W$. Conversely, a horizontal path preserves the local $S$ on each short subarc in a first-integral neighborhood by [F3]. Thus near each parameter value its image lies in the relative plaque neighborhood just shown to be reachable by such a finite word. The finite-word orbits are equivalence classes by flow reversal and concatenation, so their preimages along the path are relatively open in its interval domain. By [F4], connectedness of that interval forces one class. Hence every point horizontally reachable from $q$ lies in its finite-word orbit; the reverse inclusion follows because every word is a horizontal concatenation. steps.text: For a fixed finite word $\alpha$ of length $m\ge1$, write $F_\alpha:O_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to U$ for its endpoint map from $q$, on the open set of admissible duration tuples. Each duration derivative is a field vector transported by the later flows and is horizontal by step 1.1. Near any $s\in O_\alpha$, continuity puts the endpoint image in a neighborhood with the first integral $S$ from the hypothesis; hence $D(S\circ F_\alpha)=0$. On a small convex parameter ball, [F3] makes $S\circ F_\alpha$ constant. Choose a closed box with rational endpoints, containing $s$ in its interior and contained in that ball. Its image under $F_\alpha$ is compact by [F6], lies in one level of $S$, and has empty interior in $U$: a nonempty open subset of that image would make $S$ constant on an open set, contradicting $dS=\mu\omega\ne0$. Thus the image is a closed nowhere-dense subset of $U$. By [F5], enumerate the countable collection of all finite words and rational closed parameter boxes; for an admissible box whose compact image has empty interior record that image, and otherwise record the empty set. Include the singleton $\{q\}$ for the empty word. This explicitly defined sequence $(K_j)$ of closed nowhere-dense sets covers $\mathcal O(q)$, since every duration tuple admits the small box just constructed. No countable atlas or choice of first integrals is needed for the enumeration. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

steps.text: Let $V$ be any nonempty open subset of $U$. Choose a rational open Euclidean ball with closure contained in $V$. Recursively choose the first ball in a fixed enumeration of rational balls whose closure is inside the preceding open ball, disjoint from $K_j$, and whose radius is below $2^{-j}$. Such a ball exists because $K_j$ is closed with empty interior. If the $j$th ball has center $c_j$ and radius $r_j<2^{-j}$, then all later centers lie in its closed ball, so $|c_k-c_j|\le r_j$ for $k>j$. Thus the centers form a Cauchy sequence; [F7] gives a limit $p$ in all the nested closed balls, hence in $V$ and outside every $K_j$. Each selection is the least natural-number index satisfying explicit nonempty conditions, so it uses no choice axiom. Since the $K_j$ cover $\mathcal O(q)$, step 2.1 shows $p$ is not horizontally reachable from $q$ even by a path in $U$, and therefore not by one in $V$. This proves the asserted conclusion for every nonempty open $V$, using no global first integral or choice axiom. [given, F5, F7, F8, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎

steps.text: Fix affine coordinates $H\cong\mathbb R^k$. Closure preserves convexity without choosing approximating sequences: for $x,y\in K$ and any $\epsilon>0$, choose two points of $C$ within $\epsilon$ of them; their convex combination approximates $(1-t)x+ty$ within $\epsilon$, so this point lies in $K$. Enumerate rational $k$-tuples canonically by increasing sums of absolute numerators and positive denominators, breaking the finite ties lexicographically. Density [F6] and the open complement of $K$ show that for each $m\in\mathbb N$ at least one enumerated point lies in $B(z,\epsilon_m)\setminus K$. Let $z_m$ be the first such point. This is a uniquely specified sequence with $z_m\to z$, not a countable selection of arbitrary witnesses. [given, F3, F6, F7, construct]

steps.text: The nonempty compact set $K\cap\overline B(z_m,\|z_m-z\|+1)$ contains $z$. By [F2] and [F4], squared distance to $z_m$ attains a minimum there, and every point outside that ball is farther than the candidate $z$. Thus a nearest point $q_m\in K$ exists. It is unique: if two distinct minimizers had squared distance $d_m^2$, their midpoint would have squared distance $d_m^2-\|q_m-q'_m\|^2/4$, contradicting minimality and convexity. Consequently $(q_m)$ is also canonically determined. Since $z_m\notin K$, put $u_m=(z_m-q_m)/\|z_m-q_m\|$. Expanding the distance at $q_m+t(q-q_m)$ and letting $t\downarrow0$ gives $u_m\cdot(q-q_m)\le0$ for every $q\in K$. Also $\|q_m-z\|\le2\|z_m-z\|\to0$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

steps.text: If $C\subset\mathbb R^d$ has affine hull $H$ of dimension at most $d-2$, its orthogonal complement has dimension at least two. Choose two nonparallel nonzero normals $n_1,n_2$ orthogonal to the direction space of $H$. For each $j$, the hyperplane $\{q:n_j\cdot(q-z)=0\}$ contains $H$ and therefore supports $C$ at $z$. The two hyperplanes are distinct because their normals are not parallel. [given, F3, algebra] ∎

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: a continuous function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule]], and [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: the product rule, chain rule, and mean value theorem apply to the displayed differentiable real functions.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]: $(e^x)'=e^x$ for every real $x$.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[def-darboux-integral]]: a Riemann/Darboux integrable real function is bounded.

steps.text: By [F1], the integral defining $h(t)=\int_0^t f(s)\,ds$ exists. Continuity of $f$ gives $h'(t)=f(t)$ on $(0,T)$: the difference quotient error is bounded by $\sup_{|s-t|\le|r|}|f(s)-f(t)|$, which tends to zero as $r\to0$. By [F4], choose a finite $M$ with $0\le f\le M$. Then $|h(t)-h(s)|=|\int_s^t f|\le M|t-s|$ for all $s,t\in[0,T]$, which proves continuity at the endpoints as well as in the interior. The hypothesis gives $h'\le Lh$, so [F2]–[F3] yield $g'(t)\le0$ for $g(t)=e^{-Lt}h(t)$ on $(0,T)$. The mean value theorem makes $g$ nonincreasing; since $g(0)=0$ and $g\ge0$, $g\equiv0$ and $h\equiv0$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

steps.text: For any $t>0$, the nonnegative continuous function $f$ has integral $h(t)=0$. If $f(t_0)>0$ at any $t_0>0$, continuity gives a positive lower bound on a nonempty subinterval of $[0,t_0]$, contradicting $h(t_0)=0$. At $t=0$ the assumed inequality gives $f(0)\le0$; nonnegativity gives $f(0)=0$. Hence $f\equiv0$. [step 1.1, given] ∎

facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: each $A_x$ is supported at $x$ by a unique finite-slope plane; $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz.

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[lem-tdmath-convex-sector-closedness]]: $A_x$ is convex and closed relative to $\Gamma_i$, and its collinear order implications hold.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[lem-tdmath-sector-interior]]: every $A_x$ has nonempty ambient interior.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[lem-tdmath-relative-boundary-support]]: a convex set has a support at each relative boundary point of its closure in its affine hull.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[lem-tdmath-unique-support-inward-ray]]: at a full-dimensional convex set's boundary point with a unique support, every direction strictly toward the supporting half-space's interior enters the set's interior for all sufficiently small positive steps.

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[lem-tdmath-convex-function-local-lipschitz]]: every finite convex function on an open convex set is locally Lipschitz.

facts.label: F6
facts.text: [F6] [[lem-tdmath-integral-zero-uniqueness]]: a nonnegative continuous function bounded by a constant times its zero-start integral is identically zero.

facts.label: F7
facts.text: [F7] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: closed bounded subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space are compact.

facts.label: F8
facts.text: [F8] [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], and [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: the stated $C^1$ maps have total derivatives, and the derivative of a composition of Euclidean maps is the composition of those derivatives.

facts.label: F9
facts.text: [F9] [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]: a continuous function on a closed interval, differentiable in its interior with an integrable derivative extension, has endpoint increment equal to the integral of that derivative.

facts.label: F10
facts.text: [F10] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: a continuous real function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable.

steps.text: For fixed $x=(u_x,v_x)$, the vertical section $I_x:=\{u:(u,v_x)\in A_x\}$ is a relatively closed convex interval by [F1]. The support plane at $x$ confines it to one side of $u_x$. Its inward normal has nonzero energy component, so [F4] gives a nontrivial interior vertical segment on that side. [A1, F1, F4]

Its inward normal has nonzero energy component, so [F4] gives a nontrivial interior vertical segment on that side.

steps.text: The fiber orientation is locally constant in $v$. At any $x$, choose one vertical point just inside the supported half-space and one just outside; by [F4] the inside point can be chosen in $\operatorname{int}A_x$. Openness of $\Gamma_i$ and of the interior and exterior regions preserves these memberships on nearby fibers. Each such fiber therefore meets $\partial A_x$ between these two energy values. A support of $A_x$ at that boundary point also supports the point's own sector and so has its S2 orientation; the inside/outside placement fixes that orientation. Thus nearby fibers have the same sign as the fiber through $x$. Since $\Gamma_i$ is convex, it is connected; a locally constant two-valued sign is constant. [A1, F2, F3, F4]
steps.claim: The fiber orientation is locally constant in $v$. At any $x$, choose one vertical point just inside the supported half-space and one just outside; by [F4] the inside point can be chosen in $\operatorname{int}A_x$. Openness of $\Gamma_i$ and of the interior and exterior regions preserves these memberships on nearby fibers. Each such fiber therefore meets $\partial A_x$ between these two energy values. A support of $A_x$ at that boundary point also supports the point's own sector and so has its S2 orientation; the inside/outside placement fixes that orientation. Thus nearby fibers have the same sign as the fiber through $x$. Since $\Gamma_i$ is convex, it is connected; a locally constant two-valued sign is constant.

steps.text:
Let $u,w$ be two $C^1$ graph solutions of $Dq=-P_i(q,v)$ on a common open domain, and suppose $u(v_0)=w(v_0)$. Since $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz, choose a convex neighborhood of $(u(v_0),v_0)$ on which one Lipschitz constant $L$ works. Continuity of $u,w$ lets us choose a convex ball about $v_0$ whose closure lies in the common domain and whose two graph images stay in that neighborhood; take any $v$ in a smaller concentric ball. Put $d=v-v_0$ and $\gamma(t)=v_0+td$ for $0\le t\le1$. By [F8], $r(t)=u(\gamma(t))-w(\gamma(t))$ is $C^1$ and
$r'(t)=[-P_i(u(\gamma(t)),\gamma(t))+P_i(w(\gamma(t)),\gamma(t))]\cdot d.$
The local Lipschitz bound for $P_i$ gives $|r'(t)|\le L\|d\||r(t)|$. The derivative is continuous, hence integrable by [F10]; [F9] gives $r(t)=\int_0^t r'(s)\,ds$; hence $h(t):=|r(t)|\le L\|d\|\int_0^t h(s)\,ds$. Apply [F6] on $[0,1]$ to obtain $h=0$. Thus $u=w$ near $v_0$. Along any polygonal path in the common open domain, the set of path parameters at which equality holds is closed by continuity and open by this local result; since the path interval is connected and the set is nonempty, equality holds along the whole path. Every open connected subset of Euclidean space is polygonally connected: points reachable from a fixed point by finitely many segments in small balls form a nonempty relatively open and relatively closed set. Therefore equality extends throughout each common connected domain. [A1, F6, F8, F9, F10, given, construct]

steps.text: The convex, relatively closed interval $I_x$ contains a nontrivial segment on the inward side by step 1.1 and [F4]. Suppose it does not contain the whole open $\Gamma_i$-fiber on that side. Its endpoint $b$ toward that side then lies inside $\Gamma_i$; relative closedness puts $b$ in $I_x$, so the interval from $x$ to $b$ is a compact nondegenerate interval by [F7]. Let $x_1$ be its midpoint. Since $x_1\in A_x$, transitivity gives $A_{x_1}\subseteq A_x$. The supporting plane of $A_{x_1}$ has nonzero energy coefficient, so its vertical section lies wholly on one side of $x_1$; being contained in $I_x$, it lies in one half of $[x,b]$ and has at most half its length. It is nonempty and closed relative to $[x,b]$, hence compact. Repeat: take the midpoint $x_{k+1}$ of the current compact interval $I_{x_k}$; then $x_k\prec x_{k+1}$, so the next section is nested inside the current one and again has at most half its length. These intervals have nonempty total intersection: otherwise their open complements would cover the first compact interval, a finite subcover would do so by [F7], and nesting would make one interval empty. Their lengths tend to zero, so the intersection has a unique point $x_\infty$, still in the first interval contained in $\Gamma_i$. The midpoint recursion and this unique intersection require no selection from an arbitrary countable family. Relative closedness puts $x_\infty$ in every $A_{x_k}$, hence $A_{x_\infty}\subseteq A_{x_k}$ by transitivity. Its vertical section is therefore only $\{x_\infty\}$, contradicting the nontrivial interior vertical segment at $x_\infty$ supplied by [F4]. Thus $I_x$ contains the whole open fiber on its inward side. [A1, F1, F4, F7, step 1.1, construct]

steps.text: All states on a fixed work-coordinate fiber have the same orientation. If $x$ is oriented upward and a state $z$ above it were oriented downward, the full upward section from step 2.1 gives $x\prec z$, and the full downward section from $z$ gives $z\prec w$ for a state $w$ below $x$, contradicting the support at $x$. If a state $y$ below an upward $x$ were oriented downward, choose $z$ above $x$ with $x\prec z$; the first collinear implication in [F1], applied to $x$ between $y$ and $z$, gives $y\prec x$, contradicting the downward support at $y$. The reversed argument handles a downward $x$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

steps.text: Adopt the coordinate convention $\varepsilon_i=1$. Step 2.1 and the common orientation give $x\prec y$ exactly for $u_y\ge u_x$ at fixed $v$, with strict comparison for $u_y>u_x$. [step 3.1, step 1.2, algebra]

steps.text: Put $\rho_x=\pi_v(\partial A_x)$. At a boundary point $z\in\partial A_x$, [F3] supplies a support to $A_x$. Because $A_z\subseteq A_x$, that plane also supports $A_z$ and equals its unique S2 plane. Its finite slope gives a nonvertical inward direction; [F4] supplies nearby vertical points inside $A_x$, while the opposite side is outside by the support. Neighborhoods of one inside and one outside point show every nearby work fiber meets $\partial A_x$. Hence $\rho_x$ is open. It is connected because S3 makes $\partial A_x$ arcwise connected and projection is continuous. By step 4.1, every vertical fiber over $\rho_x$ has exactly one boundary energy; call it $u_x(v)$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 4.1]

steps.text:
For $v,v'\in\rho_x$, convexity of $A_x$ puts every convex combination of their boundary states in $A_x$. On any sufficiently small convex ball in $\rho_x$, the unique-boundary property and upward orientation make $u_x$ the least energy in each fiber. Therefore $u_x(tv+(1-t)v')\le t u_x(v)+(1-t)u_x(v')$, so $u_x$ is finite and convex there. It is locally Lipschitz by [F5]. The inward support at $(u_x(v),v)$ gives
$u_x(v')-u_x(v)\ge -P_i(u_x(v),v)\cdot(v'-v).$
The support at $(u_x(v'),v')$ gives
$u_x(v')-u_x(v)\le -P_i(u_x(v'),v')\cdot(v'-v).$
Local Lipschitz continuity of $u_x$ and $P_i$ makes the difference between these linear bounds $O(\|v'-v\|^2)$. Thus $u_x$ is differentiable with derivative $-P_i(u_x(v),v)$, and that derivative is locally Lipschitz. Hence $u_x\in C^1$ with locally Lipschitz derivative. [A1, F1, F5, F8, step 5.1]

steps.text: If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$. The boundary graphs agree at $v_y$ and solve the same differential equation. The set of $v\in\rho_y$ where $v\in\rho_x$ and $u_y(v)=u_x(v)$ is nonempty, open by step 1.3, and closed by continuity and relative closedness of $\partial A_x$. Connectedness of $\rho_y$ makes it all of $\rho_y$. This shows $\rho_y\subseteq\rho_x$. The same argument, using relative closedness of $\partial A_y$, shows $\rho_y$ is relatively closed in connected $\rho_x$; it is relatively open because both projections are open. Hence $\rho_x=\rho_y$ and the boundary graphs agree. In particular $x\in\partial A_y$, so $y\prec x$; together with $y\in A_x$ and transitivity this gives $A_x=A_y$. [A1, F1, step 6.1, step 1.3] ∎

facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]: On each designated open single-phase chart, the entropy representative is $C^2$ and its finite partial derivative $S_{c,U}$ at fixed $V,n$ is strictly positive. This is an adopted physical premise, not a proved physical law.

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]], and [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]: $D_c$ consists of dimensionless SI numerical coordinates, and $\Phi_c$ maps them to the physical-coordinate chart $\Omega$; $S_c(U,V,n)$ denotes the entropy composed with $\Phi_c^{-1}$. The energy $U$ is evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame. The state-domain definition does not assert that every ambient coordinate tuple is physically realizable.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]: $T_c=1/S_{c,U}$, $p_c=T_cS_{c,V}$, and $\mu_{c,j}=-T_cS_{c,n_j}$, with the other physical coordinates held fixed in each partial derivative.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: For differentiable maps on open Euclidean domains, differentiation of a composition obeys the total-derivative chain rule.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: A scalar map is $C^2$ when its coordinate partial derivatives through order two exist and are continuous.

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]]: Finite sums and products and compositions of $C^1$ Euclidean maps are $C^1$.

facts.label: L1
facts.text: [L1] [[thm-tdmath-local-implicit-rank]]: The supplier's Statement says that a $C^1$ map on an open Euclidean set with a zero and an invertible derivative minor has a unique local $C^1$ graph representation, with derivative $D\varphi=-(D_vF)^{-1}D_uF$. In its scalar case, apply it to $G(U,s,V,n)=S_c(U,V,n)-s$, placing $U$ in the dependent-coordinate block; $G_U=S_{c,U}>0$. The supplier currently has draft status and supplies a $C^1$ graph, not a $C^2$ one; the argument below derives the extra regularity from the adopted $C^2$ entropy premise.

steps.text: Put $y=(V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ and choose an open interval $J$ around $s_0=S_c(U_0,y_0)$. On the open set where $(U,y)\in\Omega$ and $s\in J$, define $G(U,s,y)=S_c(U,y)-s$. By [A1] and [F1], this map is $C^1$, $G(U_0,s_0,y_0)=0$, and its $1\times1$ derivative minor in the $U$ coordinate equals $S_{c,U}(U_0,y_0)>0$. Since the total number of coordinates is $r+3>1$, the scalar graph case of [L1] applies after placing $U$ in the dependent block. Conditional on that draft supplier, it gives a unique local $C^1$ function $U=\mathcal U_c(s,y)$ solving $S_c(\mathcal U_c(s,y),y)=s$. [given, A1, F1, L1, construct]
steps.claim: Put $y=(V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ and choose an open interval $J$ around $s_0=S_c(U_0,y_0)$. On the open set where $(U,y)\in\Omega$ and $s\in J$, define $G(U,s,y)=S_c(U,y)-s$. By [A1] and [F1], this map is $C^1$, $G(U_0,s_0,y_0)=0$, and its $1\times1$ derivative minor in the $U$ coordinate equals $S_{c,U}(U_0,y_0)>0$. Since the total number of coordinates is $r+3>1$, the scalar graph case of [L1] applies after placing $U$ in the dependent block. Conditional on that draft supplier, it gives a unique local $C^1$ function $U=\mathcal U_c(s,y)$ solving $S_c(\mathcal U_c(s,y),y)=s$.

steps.text: Differentiate $S_c(\mathcal U_c(s,y),y)=s$ in each coordinate of $(s,y)$ using [F3]. Writing $\Psi(s,y)=(\mathcal U_c(s,y),y)$, the resulting first-derivative identities are $\mathcal U_{c,s}=1/(S_{c,U}\circ\Psi)$ and $\mathcal U_{c,y_j}=-(S_{c,y_j}\circ\Psi)/(S_{c,U}\circ\Psi)$. Each partial $S_{c,U},S_{c,y_j}$ is $C^1$ by [A1],[F4], and $\Psi$ is $C^1$ by [L1]. Thus their compositions with $\Psi$ are $C^1$ by [F3],[F5]. For a positive scalar $z$, $\rho(z)=1/z$ is $C^1$: its difference quotient is $[\rho(z+h)-\rho(z)]/h=-1/(z(z+h))\to-1/z^2$, a continuous derivative on $z>0$. Since $S_{c,U}\circ\Psi>0$, the displayed expressions for every first partial of $\mathcal U_c$ are $C^1$ by [F5]. Hence all second coordinate partials of $\mathcal U_c$ exist and are continuous, so $\mathcal U_c$ is $C^2$ by [F4]. [given, A1, F3, F4, F5, L1, step 1.1, algebra]

Writing $\Psi(s,y)=(\mathcal U_c(s,y),y)$, the resulting first-derivative identities are $\mathcal U_{c,s}=1/(S_{c,U}\circ\Psi)$ and $\mathcal U_{c,y_j}=-(S_{c,y_j}\circ\Psi)/(S_{c,U}\circ\Psi)$. Each partial $S_{c,U},S_{c,y_j}$ is $C^1$ by [A1],[F4], and $\Psi$ is $C^1$ by [L1]. Thus their compositions with $\Psi$ are $C^1$ by [F3],[F5]. For a positive scalar $z$, $\rho(z)=1/z$ is $C^1$: its difference quotient is $[\rho(z+h)-\rho(z)]/h=-1/(z(z+h))\to-1/z^2$, a continuous derivative on $z>0$. Since $S_{c,U}\circ\Psi>0$, the displayed expressions for every first partial of $\mathcal U_c$ are $C^1$ by [F5]. Hence all second coordinate partials of $\mathcal U_c$ exist and are continuous, so $\mathcal U_c$ is $C^2$ by [F4].

steps.text: By [F2], $T_c=1/S_{c,U}$, $p_c=T_cS_{c,V}$, and $\mu_{c,j}=-T_cS_{c,n_j}$. The derivative identities in step 2.1 therefore give $\mathcal U_{c,s}=T_c$, $\mathcal U_{c,V}=-p_c$, and $\mathcal U_{c,n_j}=\mu_{c,j}$, with the other coordinates held fixed. [F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
steps.claim: By [F2], $T_c=1/S_{c,U}$, $p_c=T_cS_{c,V}$, and $\mu_{c,j}=-T_cS_{c,n_j}$. The derivative identities in step 2.1 therefore give $\mathcal U_{c,s}=T_c$, $\mathcal U_{c,V}=-p_c$, and $\mathcal U_{c,n_j}=\mu_{c,j}$, with the other coordinates held fixed.

facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]: For a stable equilibrium of the declared isolated compound, the model adopts an attained global maximum of the summed entropy on the exact feasible endpoint set. It assumes attainment; it proves no dynamics or uniqueness.

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]: $\mathcal F$ is the declared subset of the product of constituent state domains satisfying the specified totals and exactly the allowed exchanges; retained barriers fix the associated coordinates.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] and [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]: On the selected smooth single-phase charts the entropy has finite $C^2$ derivatives and $S_U>0$, and independent separated constituents have additive entropy and the declared additive extensive coordinates.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[def-td-thermal-contact-constraints]]: A diathermal contact permits thermal energy transfer between constituents while forbidding matter transfer and mechanical or composition work across that contact. Here it supports the energy-exchange variation only; [F1] and the stated bilateral-feasibility hypothesis govern the other named exchange channels.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]: Each $D_{c_i}$ uses dimensionless coordinates, and its physical chart is the image under $\Phi_{c_i}$; the entropy on physical tuples is the composition with $\Phi_{c_i}^{-1}$. Write $(U_i^*,V_i^*,n_i^*)=\Phi_{c_i}(x_i^*)$ for the physical SI tuple of subsystem $i$. The derivative identities are $S_{i,U}=1/T_i$, $S_{i,V}=p_i/T_i$, and $S_{i,n_j}=-\mu_{i,j}/T_i$, with other physical coordinates fixed.

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[def-td-si-quantities]]: The coordinates $U,V,n_j$ use joules, cubic metres, and moles; $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ in pascals, and $\mu_j$ in joules per mole.

facts.label: A2
facts.text: [A2] [[post-td-mechanical-conjugate-identification]]: For the declared quasistatic frictionless piston, derivative pressure equals force per area and $\delta W_{\mathrm{on}}=-p\,dV$. This is an adopted coupling, not a mathematical consequence.

facts.label: L1
facts.text: [L1] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: For differentiable maps between open Euclidean sets, the derivative of a composition is the composition of the derivatives. This is the mathematical chain rule used to differentiate entropy along each feasible one-parameter exchange.

steps.text: For energy exchange choose an arbitrary sufficiently small $h$ joules and the feasible physical-coordinate curves $z_A(t)=(U_A^*+t h,V_A^*,n_A^*)$, $z_B(t)=(U_B^*-t h,V_B^*,n_B^*)$ for $t$ near $0$. Their state-domain coordinates are $\Phi_{c_A}^{-1}(z_A(t))$ and $\Phi_{c_B}^{-1}(z_B(t))$; openness of the physical charts and the bilateral-feasibility hypothesis make both signs locally feasible. By [A1], $g(t):=S_A(z_A(t))+S_B(z_B(t))$ has a local maximum at $0$; [F1] and [F3] specify that this thermal energy exchange is allowed. For $t>0$, $(g(t)-g(0))/t\le0$; for $t<0$, the same quotient is $\ge0$. Its derivative exists by [F2], so the two one-sided limits force $g'(0)=0$. The chain rule [L1] gives $g'(0)=h(S_{A,U}-S_{B,U})$. Since $h\ne0$, $S_{A,U}=S_{B,U}$. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, L1, construct]
steps.claim: For energy exchange choose an arbitrary sufficiently small $h$ joules and the feasible physical-coordinate curves $z_A(t)=(U_A^*+t h,V_A^*,n_A^*)$, $z_B(t)=(U_B^*-t h,V_B^*,n_B^*)$ for $t$ near $0$. Their state-domain coordinates are $\Phi_{c_A}^{-1}(z_A(t))$ and $\Phi_{c_B}^{-1}(z_B(t))$; openness of the physical charts and the bilateral-feasibility hypothesis make both signs locally feasible. By [A1], $g(t):=S_A(z_A(t))+S_B(z_B(t))$ has a local maximum at $0$; [F1] and [F3] specify that this thermal energy exchange is allowed. For $t>0$, $(g(t)-g(0))/t\le0$; for $t<0$, the same quotient is $\ge0$. Its derivative exists by [F2], so the two one-sided limits force $g'(0)=0$. The chain rule [L1] gives $g'(0)=h(S_{A,U}-S_{B,U})$. Since $h\ne0$, $S_{A,U}=S_{B,U}$.

steps.text: By [F4], $S_{i,U}=1/T_i$ for $i=A,B$. The temperatures are finite and positive, so equality of their reciprocals gives $T_A=T_B$. [given, F4, step 1.1, algebra]
steps.claim: By [F4], $S_{i,U}=1/T_i$ for $i=A,B$. The temperatures are finite and positive, so equality of their reciprocals gives $T_A=T_B$.

steps.text: If volume exchange is permitted, hold the energy and species partitions fixed and vary $V_A(t)=V_A^*+t k$, $V_B(t)=V_B^*-t k$ for an arbitrary sufficiently small nonzero volume increment $k$. The same two-sided local-maximum argument in step 1.1 gives $0=k(S_{A,V}-S_{B,V})$, hence $S_{A,V}=S_{B,V}$. By [F4], $p_A/T_A=p_B/T_B$. When energy exchange is also permitted, step 2.1 gives $T_A=T_B>0$, hence $p_A=p_B$. By [A2], this is equality of the two derivative pressures with their respective mechanical piston pressures whenever that coupling applies to each subsystem. facts.text: [A1] Ideal thermal reservoir: its energy $E_R$ ranges in an open interval and its entropy is $S_R(E_R)=S_{R,0}+E_R/T_0$ there. Heat $Q$ positive into the system changes its energy by $\Delta E_R=-Q$, so $\Delta S_R=-Q/T_0$.

facts.label: A2
facts.text: [A2] Ideal pressure store: at fixed external pressure $p_0$, its stored energy changes by $p_0\Delta V$ when the system volume changes by $\Delta V$; the only system work is $W_{\mathrm{on}}=-p_0\Delta V$. The store's entropy is constant. At fixed volume this store is absent. No other work coordinate or matter transfer is admitted.

facts.label: A3
facts.text: [A3] The system and bath, with the pressure store when present, form an isolated compound with fixed total energy. In the fixed-volume case $\Delta U+\Delta E_R=0$; in the fixed-pressure case $\Delta U+\Delta E_R+p_0\Delta V=0$. These are explicit ideal-environment constraints; they do not follow from units.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[post-td-macroscopic-second-law]]: For the admitted isolated compound with its named auxiliaries and equilibrium endpoints, $\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}\ge0$.

facts.label: F3
