facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[def-td-response-functions]]: $C_V=(\partial U/\partial T)_{V,n}$, $C_p=(\partial H/\partial T)_{p,n}$, $\kappa_T=-V^{-1}(\partial V/\partial p)_{T,n}$, and $\alpha_p=V^{-1}(\partial V/\partial T)_{p,n}$; the definitions assert no response identities.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[pthm-td-potential-differentials]]: $dF=-s\,dT-p\,dV+\sum_j\mu_j\,dn_j$ and $dH=T\,ds+V\,dp+\sum_j\mu_j\,dn_j$ on valid charts.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[pthm-td-maxwell-relations]]: $s_V|_{T,n}=p_T|_{V,n}$ on the Helmholtz chart.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: Derivatives of compositions obey the total-derivative chain rule.

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[thm-chain-sum-product-and-composition-rules-for-banach-derivatives]]: The derivative of a product of differentiable scalar maps is the sum of the two product terms.

steps.text: At fixed $V,n$, $U=F+Ts$ and $F_T=-s$ from [F2], so the product rule [F5] gives $C_V=U_T|_{V,n}=T s_T|_{V,n}$. At fixed $p,n$, $dH=T\,ds+V\,dp$ from [F2], hence $C_p=H_T|_{p,n}=T s_T|_{p,n}$. [given, F2, F5, algebra]

steps.text: On the valid isothermal response inverse, write $V=V(T,p,n)$, so $p(T,V(T,p,n),n)=p$, where the rightmost $p$ is the independent pressure coordinate. Differentiating in that pressure coordinate at fixed $T,n$ gives $1=p_V|_{T,n}V_p|_{T,n}$. By [F1], $V_p|_{T,n}=-V\kappa_T$, hence $p_V|_{T,n}=-1/(V\kappa_T)$. Differentiating the same identity in $T$ at fixed $p,n$ gives $0=p_T|_{V,n}+p_V|_{T,n}V_T|_{p,n}$. Again by [F1], $V_T|_{p,n}=V\alpha_p$, so $p_T|_{V,n}=\alpha_p/\kappa_T$. The stated inverse chart and $\kappa_T>0$ make these derivatives and reciprocals valid. [given, F1, F4, algebra]

facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] $C_V>0$ and $\kappa_T>0$ are explicit response hypotheses on this chart; they are not inferred from notation alone.

facts.label: F1

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[def-td-isentropic-compressibility]]: $\kappa_S=-V^{-1}V_p|_{s,n}$ on a valid isentropic inverse chart.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[pthm-td-potential-differentials]]: $dU=T\,ds-p\,dV$ and $dH=T\,ds+V\,dp$ on the named valid charts.

facts.label: F4

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[pthm-td-heat-capacity-relation]]: $C_p-C_V=TV\alpha_p^2/\kappa_T$ on the stated stable response chart.

facts.label: F6
facts.text: [F6] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: Differentiating a composition gives the usual total-derivative chain rule.

steps.text: By [F1], $C_V=U_T|_{V,n}$. On the fixed-volume path in the Helmholtz chart, [F3] gives $dU=T\,ds$; composing with the chart map and applying [F6] yields $C_V=T s_T|_{V,n}$. Likewise, by [F1], $C_p=H_T|_{p,n}$, and on the fixed-pressure path in the Gibbs chart [F3] gives $dH=T\,ds$; the chain rule yields $C_p=T s_T|_{p,n}$. Thus at fixed $n$, $ds=(C_V/T)\,dT+p_T|_{V,n}\,dV$. Along an isentrope $ds=0$, the valid chart gives $T_V|_{s,n}=-T p_T|_{V,n}/C_V$. [given, A1, F1, F3, F6, algebra]

Substitution into step 2.1 yields $p_V|_{s,n}=p_V|_{T,n}(C_p/C_V)$. Since $p_V|_{T,n}<0$ and $C_V>0$, [F5] also gives $C_p=C_V-T(p_T|_{V,n})^2/p_V|_{T,n}\ge C_V>0$, hence $p_V|_{s,n}<0$. facts.text: [F1] [[pthm-td-potential-differentials]]: On a valid chart, $dH=T\,ds+V\,dp+\sum_j\mu_j\,dn_j$ and $dG=-s\,dT+V\,dp+\sum_j\mu_j\,dn_j$.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[pthm-td-maxwell-relations]]: For the Gibbs chart, $s_p|_{T,n}=-V_T|_{p,n}$.

facts.label: F3

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]: $H=U+pV$ and $G=H-Ts$ on their local natural-variable charts.

facts.label: F5

steps.text: At fixed $n$, write $ds=s_T|_{p,n}\,dT+s_p|_{T,n}\,dp$ in [F1]. The enthalpy $H$ and chart are those of [F4]. Since $C_p=H_T|_{p,n}$ and $dH=T\,ds+V\,dp$, the coefficient of $dT$ gives $C_p=T s_T|_{p,n}$. Therefore $dH=C_p\,dT+(T s_p|_{T,n}+V)\,dp$. [given, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[def-td-reservoir-cycle]]: In engine mode $Q[P]=Q_h-Q_c$, $W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]=-W_{\mathrm{out}}$, the hot and cold bath energy changes are $-Q_h$ and $+Q_c$, their endpoint entropy changes are $-Q_h/T_h$ and $+Q_c/T_c$, the working system returns to its initial state, and the work store gains $\Delta E_w=W_{\mathrm{out}}$ with zero entropy change. The full compound has the admitted equilibrium endpoint record and additive entropy split required by the definition.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[post-td-first-law-energy]]: For an admitted closed fixed-constitution process with zero endpoint changes in separately tracked center-of-mass kinetic and external-potential energies, $\Delta U=Q[P]+W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]$.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[post-td-macroscopic-second-law]]: For an admitted isolated compound process with equilibrium endpoints and the declared additive total entropy, $\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}\ge0$; an admitted reversible operation has $\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}=0$.

steps.text: The working system returns to its initial state, so $\Delta U=0$. Applying [F2] with [F1] gives $0=Q_h-Q_c-W_{\mathrm{out}}$, hence $W_{\mathrm{out}}=Q_h-Q_c$ and $\eta=1-Q_c/Q_h$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

steps.text:
The hot bath loses energy $Q_h$, the cold bath gains $Q_c$, and their entropy slopes are constant. Thus their entropy changes are $-Q_h/T_h$ and $Q_c/T_c$. The working system and work store have zero entropy change, so [F3] gives
$
-\frac{Q_h}{T_h}+\frac{Q_c}{T_c}=\Delta S_{\mathrm{tot}}\ge0.
$
[given, F1, F3, algebra]

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[def-td-si-quantities]]: $k_{\mathrm B}>0$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, so each exponent is dimensionless and $S_G$ is in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]: The positive $T$ parameter is interpreted as absolute thermodynamic temperature on its declared chart; the finite Gibbs preparation is a separate model branch.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[def-natural-logarithm]]: $\log$ is the natural logarithm with domain $(0,\infty)$.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: $\log$ is continuous and strictly increasing, and $\log(1/x)=-\log x$ for $x>0$.

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[thm-exponential-limits-and-range]]: $\exp(x)\to0$ as $x\to-\infty$.

facts.label: F6
facts.text: [F6] [[thm-logarithm-slower-than-every-positive-power]]: $\log x/x\to0$ as $x\to+\infty$.

steps.text: For each excited state $i\notin G:=\{i:E_i=E_0\}$, $(E_i-E_0)/(k_{\mathrm B}T)\to+\infty$, so $w_i(T)\to0$ by [F5]. Ground-state weights are $1$. Since there are finitely many states, $Z(T)\to g$, each ground-state probability tends to $1/g$, and each excited-state probability tends to $0$. [given, F1, F2, F5, algebra]

steps.text: For any $x\in\ell^2(I)$ and $\epsilon>0$, the finite-subset supremum supplies a finite $F$ whose square sum differs from the total by less than $\epsilon^2$. For every finite $G\subset I\setminus F$, its square sum is at most that difference, by applying the total bound to $F\cup G$. Hence the norm of the omitted tail is at most $\epsilon$. Finite-coordinate truncations therefore approximate $x$ and lie in $D(H_E)$ by step 1.2, proving density. If $I$ is empty all spaces and maps are zero, and the same statements hold directly. facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] $A$ is finite, $q\ge1$, $e_j\in\mathbb R$, $\beta\in\mathbb R$, and $\delta_N\ge q\sum_j|e_j|$ with $\delta_N/N\to0$.

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[def-tdmath-finite-site-shell-and-canonical-law]]: configurations have additive energies, the canonical probabilities are $p_j=e^{-\beta e_j}/Z_1$, and the shell law is uniform when the shell is nonempty.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[def-finite-sum]] and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: the finite sums and logarithms obey the usual finite distributive and product identities.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and [[def-natural-logarithm]]: exponential weights are positive and logarithm is the inverse of the positive real exponential.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: $\log$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)$, has derivative $1/x$, and $\log x=\int_1^xdt/t$.

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: the finite-dimensional probability simplex is compact, so every sequence in it has a convergent subsequence.

steps.text: For a type $t_j=n_j/N$, the number of configurations of that type is $M(n)=N!/\prod_j n_j!$. The increasing function $\log x$ gives $$\int_1^m\log x\,dx\le\log(m!)\le\int_1^{m+1}\log x\,dx\quad(m\ge1).$$ Evaluating the antiderivative $x\log x-x$ and using $\log(1+1/m)\le1/m$ shows $\log(m!)=m\log m-m+O(\log(m+1)+1)$ with an absolute constant; the case $m=0$ uses $0!=1$ and $0\log0=0$. Subtracting the $q$ denominator estimates from the numerator estimate gives a constant $C_q$ such that $$NH(t)-C_q\log(N+1)-C_q\le\log M(n)\le NH(t)+C_q\log(N+1)+C_q,$$ where $H(t)=-\sum_jt_j\log t_j$. The sharper upper bound $M(n)\le e^{NH(t)}$ follows by expanding $1=(\sum_jt_j)^N$ and retaining the nonnegative terms with counts $n$. [A1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

The sharper upper bound $M(n)\le e^{NH(t)}$ follows by expanding $1=(\sum_jt_j)^N$ and retaining the nonnegative terms with counts $n$.

steps.text: For any probability vector $t$, define $D(t\Vert p)=\sum_{j:t_j>0}t_j\log(t_j/p_j)$. Since $\log u\le u-1$ for $u>0$ (integrate $1/x$ on either side of $1$ using [F4]), $$D(t\Vert p)\ge\sum_{j:t_j>0}(t_j-p_j)=1-\sum_{j:t_j>0}p_j\ge0.$$ Equality forces every $p_j$ to be included and each ratio $t_j/p_j$ to equal $1$, so $t=p$. Also $\log p_j=-\beta e_j-\log Z_1$, hence $D(t\Vert p)=-H(t)+\beta\sum_jt_je_j+\log Z_1$. In particular, among types of exact mean energy $E$, entropy is at most $H(p)$, with equality only at $p$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4]

steps.text: Round down $Np_j$ for $j<q$ and put the remainder in $n_q$. Then $|n_j/N-p_j|\le1/N$ for $j<q$ and $|n_q/N-p_q|\le(q-1)/N$. Thus $$\left|\sum_jn_je_j-NE\right|\le\sum_{j<q}|e_j|+(q-1)|e_q|\le q\sum_j|e_j|\le\delta_N.$$ This type belongs to $\Gamma_N$, proving nonemptiness. Its frequencies tend to $p$, and continuity of $-x\log x$ at zero gives $H(t)\to H(p)$. By the lower bound in 1.1, the shell contains at least $\exp(NH(p)-o(N))$ configurations. [A1, F1, F4, step 1.1]

steps.text: Fix $\epsilon>0$. There are $\eta>0$ and $\tau>0$ such that $|t-p|\ge\epsilon$ and $|\sum_jt_je_j-E|\le\tau$ imply $H(t)\le H(p)-\eta$. Otherwise, choosing tolerance $1/n$ and entropy at least $H(p)-1/n$, compactness [F5] gives a subsequential limit $t_*$ with mean $E$, distance at least $\epsilon$, and entropy $H(p)$. Continuity of $H$ and the equality characterization in step 1.2 force $t_*=p$, a contradiction. For large $N$, $\delta_N/N\le\tau$; therefore every shell type outside the $\epsilon$-ball has entropy at most $H(p)-\eta$. There are at most $(N+1)^q$ types, and 1.1 bounds the number of configurations of each by $\exp[NH(t)]$. Dividing this upper bound by the shell lower bound in step 2.1 shows that the shell probability of types outside that ball tends to zero exponentially. Thus the random type converges in probability to $p$. [A1, F1, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2]

Thus the random type converges in probability to $p$.

steps.text: Conditional on a type $t$, a uniform configuration is a uniformly ordered list of its $N$ labeled positions. Couple the first $k$ draws without replacement with $k$ independent uniform position draws: if the independent positions are distinct, keep them; if not, replace them by an independently chosen uniform ordered distinct $k$-tuple. The resulting tuple is uniform among distinct positions and agrees with the original draws except on the collision event. A union bound over the $\binom{k}{2}$ pairs gives collision probability at most $k(k-1)/(2N)$. Hence the type-conditional label marginal differs in total variation from $t^{\otimes k}$ by at most this quantity. Since $t\to p$ in probability and each of the finitely many probabilities $\prod_{r=1}^k t_{i_r}$ is continuous and bounded on the simplex, averaging over shell types proves convergence of the marginal to $p^{\otimes k}$ in total variation. [A1, F1, F5, step 3.1, algebra]

steps.text:
The rounded shell type and lower bound in step 2.1 give $\liminf_NN^{-1}\log|\Gamma_N|\ge H(p)$. For any shell type $t$, step 1.2 gives the exact identity
$$H(t)=H(p)+\beta\left(\sum_jt_je_j-E\right)-D(t\Vert p)\le H(p)+|\beta|\delta_N/N.$$
There are at most $(N+1)^q$ types, and step 1.1 bounds each multiplicity by $e^{NH(t)}$. Therefore
$$|\Gamma_N|\le(N+1)^q\exp\!\left(NH(p)+|\beta|\delta_N\right).$$
Since $q\log(N+1)/N\to0$ and $\delta_N/N\to0$, the limsup is at most $H(p)$. Together with the lower bound this proves the entropy-density limit, including $\beta=0$, without invoking a nonexistent compactness step. [A1, F1, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] AC is adopted; the actual draft supplier statement [[thm-tdmath-general-trace-gibbs-model]] assumes a nonzero complex Hilbert space, self-adjoint $A$ with spectral support in $[a,\infty)$, $\beta>0$, and positive trace-class Gibbs operator $K_\beta$. Its first clause supplies a finite or countable complete orthonormal basis of eigenvectors $Au_j=E_ju_j$, finite multiplicity for each energy, and a positive finite partition trace. Its complete proof is present as draft; the dependency is used conditionally.

facts.label: A2
facts.text: [A2] $\rho$ is positive trace class with trace one; $\hbar>0$ is fixed and the phase is $e^{-iE_jt/\hbar}$.

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[def-trace-class-operator]]: trace-class operators have finite trace norm and form the space on which the trace and trace norm are defined.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]: trace class is a Banach space, and $\|ARB\|_1\le\|A\|\|R\|_1\|B\|$ for bounded $A,B$.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[lem-finite-rank-compressions-converge-in-trace-norm]]: if finite-rank orthogonal projections converge strongly to the identity on a separable Hilbert space, their two-sided compressions of a trace-class operator converge in trace norm.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[thm-trace-of-a-positive-operator-is-the-sum-of-its-eigenvalues]] and [[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]: positive trace is the sum of diagonal eigenbasis entries, and the trace is basis independent.

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[thm-cyclicity-of-the-trace]]: for trace-class $S$ and bounded $B$, $\operatorname{Tr}(SB)=\operatorname{Tr}(BS)$.

facts.label: F6
facts.text: [F6] [[def-complex-exponential]], [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], and [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]: the complex exponential is continuous, has derivative itself, obeys addition, and has unit modulus on imaginary arguments. [[thm-ftc-second-part]] evaluates its real and imaginary antiderivatives componentwise on compact real intervals.

facts.label: F7
facts.text: [F7] [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]: the Hilbert inner product is linear in the first argument.

steps.text: Each multiplier $e^{-iE_jt/\hbar}$ has modulus one by [F6]. Thus $U_t$ preserves the norm of finite linear combinations of the complete orthonormal basis; it extends by density to an isometry on the Hilbert space. The similarly defined $U_{-t}$ is its inverse, so $U_t$ is unitary and depends continuously on $t$ on each finite-dimensional energy span. The arguments $E_jt/\hbar$ are dimensionless. [A1, A2, F6, F7]

Thus $U_t$ preserves the norm of finite linear combinations of the complete orthonormal basis; it extends by density to an isometry on the Hilbert space. The similarly defined $U_{-t}$ is its inverse, so $U_t$ is unitary and depends continuously on $t$ on each finite-dimensional energy span. The arguments $E_jt/\hbar$ are dimensionless.

steps.text: By [F2], $\rho_t=U_t\rho U_t^*$ is trace class. It is positive because $\langle\rho_t x,x\rangle=\langle\rho U_t^*x,U_t^*x\rangle\ge0$, and cyclicity [F5] gives $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_t=\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. [A2, F2, F5, F7, step 1.1]
steps.claim: By [F2], $\rho_t=U_t\rho U_t^*$ is trace class. It is positive because $\langle\rho_t x,x\rangle=\langle\rho U_t^*x,U_t^*x\rangle\ge0$, and cyclicity [F5] gives $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_t=\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$.

steps.text: Enumerate the distinct energy eigenspaces and let $P_N$ project onto the first $N$ of them, with $P_N=I$ after the list is exhausted if it is finite. Their union spans the eigenbasis, so $P_N\to I$ strongly. The Hilbert space is separable by the countable complete basis in [A1]. Therefore [F3] gives $\|P_N\rho P_N-\rho\|_1\to0$. Unitary invariance of trace norm follows from [F2] in both directions: $\|U_tRU_t^*\|_1\le\|R\|_1$ and $R=U_t^*(U_tRU_t^*)U_t$ gives the reverse inequality. Consequently $$\|U_tP_N\rho P_NU_t^*-\rho_t\|_1=\|P_N\rho P_N-\rho\|_1$$ uniformly in $t$. [A1, A2, F2, F3, step 1.1]

Their union spans the eigenbasis, so $P_N\to I$ strongly. The Hilbert space is separable by the countable complete basis in [A1]. Therefore [F3] gives $\|P_N\rho P_N-\rho\|_1\to0$. steps.text: For fixed $N$, the matrix of $U_tP_N\rho P_NU_t^*$ on its finite-dimensional range has continuous entries, hence is continuous in trace norm. Step 2.2 makes $\rho_t$ a uniform trace-norm limit on compact time intervals of these continuous maps; therefore $t\mapsto\rho_t$ is trace-norm continuous. On $[0,T]$ it is uniformly continuous. Riemann sums for a uniformly continuous Banach-valued function are Cauchy: two sums are compared on a common refinement and their difference is bounded by $T$ times the modulus of continuity at the larger mesh. Completeness in [F2] supplies the trace-class integral and its usual norm bound. [F2, step 2.2]

Step 2.2 makes $\rho_t$ a uniform trace-norm limit on compact time intervals of these continuous maps; therefore $t\mapsto\rho_t$ is trace-norm continuous. On $[0,T]$ it is uniformly continuous. steps.text: In the eigenbasis, the $(i,j)$ matrix entry of $U_tP_N\rho P_NU_t^*$ is $\langle\rho u_j,u_i\rangle e^{i(E_j-E_i)t/\hbar}$. Its time-average factor is $1$ if $E_i=E_j$; if $E_i\ne E_j$, direct integration using [F6] gives absolute value at most $2\hbar/(T|E_j-E_i|)$, which tends to zero. Since the compression is finite dimensional, entrywise convergence implies trace-norm convergence. Hence the finite compressed average tends to $\sum_{E\text{ among the first }N}P_E\rho P_E$. [A1, A2, F6, F7, step 3.1]
steps.claim: In the eigenbasis, the $(i,j)$ matrix entry of $U_tP_N\rho P_NU_t^*$ is $\langle\rho u_j,u_i\rangle e^{i(E_j-E_i)t/\hbar}$. Its time-average factor is $1$ if $E_i=E_j$; if $E_i\ne E_j$, direct integration using [F6] gives absolute value at most $2\hbar/(T|E_j-E_i|)$, which tends to zero. Since the compression is finite dimensional, entrywise convergence implies trace-norm convergence. Hence the finite compressed average tends to $\sum_{E\text{ among the first }N}P_E\rho P_E$.

steps.text: Each block $P_E\rho P_E$ is positive trace class. The sum of their traces is $$\sum_E\sum_{u_j\in\operatorname{ran}P_E}\langle\rho u_j,u_j\rangle =\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$$ by [F4] and the complete basis in [A1]. Therefore their finite partial sums are Cauchy in trace norm: for a positive finite block tail its trace norm equals its trace, and the scalar trace tail tends to zero. Their limit $\rho_{\rm diag}$ exists in trace norm, is positive, and has trace one. [A1, A2, F1, F4, step 4.1]

facts.text: [A1] $u_1,u_2$ are orthonormal, $E_1\ne E_2$, $\hbar>0$, and $\rho=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$ for $\psi=(u_1+u_2)/\sqrt2$.

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]], and [[thm-ftc-second-part]]: imaginary exponential phases have modulus one, their derivatives give the explicit antiderivative, and the real and imaginary integrals are evaluated componentwise. The finite-dimensional Cesàro limit is computed here and does not invoke an uninstantiated infinite-dimensional Gibbs-spectrum theorem.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and [[def-complex-exponential]]: orthonormal coordinates use the Hilbert inner product and phase factors have unit modulus.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: $\log$ is continuous on positive reals and $\log2$ is finite.

steps.text: The unitary evolution sends $\psi$ to $(e^{-iE_1t/\hbar}u_1+e^{-iE_2t/\hbar}u_2)/\sqrt2$, which remains a unit vector by [F2]. Its rank-one density has eigenvalues $1,0$, so its entropy is $-k_B(1\log1+0\log0)=0$ for every $t$. [A1, F2, algebra]

steps.text: The two energy eigenspaces are one-dimensional. The matrix entry between them is an exponential with nonzero frequency; by [F1] its average has magnitude at most $\hbar/(T|E_1-E_2|)$ and tends to zero. The diagonal entries remain $1/2$, so the direct finite-dimensional average yields $\rho_{\rm diag}=\tfrac12P_1+\tfrac12P_2$. Its eigenvalues are $(1/2,1/2)$, so $$S(\rho_{\rm diag})=-k_B\left(\tfrac12\log\tfrac12+\tfrac12\log\tfrac12\right)=k_B\log2.$$ Since every $S(\rho_t)=0$, the time average of instantaneous entropy is exactly zero. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.1]

steps.text: In the basis $(u_1,u_2)$, $\bar\rho_T$ has diagonal entries $1/2$ and off-diagonal entry $$c_T=\frac1{2T}\int_0^T e^{-i(E_1-E_2)t/\hbar}\,dt,$$ whose magnitude is at most $\hbar/(T|E_1-E_2|)$ by direct integration. Its eigenvalues are $1/2\pm|c_T|$, so both tend to $1/2$. Continuity of $x\mapsto-x\log x$ at $1/2$ gives $S(\bar\rho_T)\to k_B\log2$. Thus entropy of the averaged state has a nonzero limit even though the averaged instantaneous entropy remains zero. [A1, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] Ideal thermal reservoir: throughout its admitted energy interval, $S_R(E_R)=S_{R,0}+E_R/T_0$, with $E_R$ in joules and $S_R$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The same compound record $\widehat P$ has $\Delta E_R[\widehat P]=-Q[P_s]$, hence $\Delta S_R[\widehat P]=-Q[P_s]/T_0$.

facts.label: A2
facts.text: [A2] Ideal pressure store: for every $(x,y_R,y_B)\in\mathcal F$, its energy satisfies $E_B(y_B)-p_0V_c(x)=C_B$ for one fixed constant $C_B$, and its entropy is constant on the admitted store states. The extension record satisfies $\Delta E_B[\widehat P]=p_0\Delta V_c[P_s]$; the only work on the system record is $W_{\rm on}[P_s]=-p_0\Delta V_c[P_s]$.

facts.label: A3
facts.text: [A3] The system, reservoir, and pressure store form the isolated compound for the adopted macroscopic second-law and stable-equilibrium model. The endpoint association $\rho_{\widehat P}$ has both values in $\mathcal F$; total energy is fixed on $\mathcal F$ and separated constituent entropies add.

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]: $P_s$ is one admitted closed system process record with endpoints $x_{P_s}^\pm$; its protocol assigns the same record's heat and work functionals $Q[P_s]$ and $W_{\rm on}[P_s]$ in joules. The isolated-compound record $\widehat P$ records the auxiliary endpoint states and extension of that system record.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[post-td-first-law-energy]]: For the admitted closed system record $P_s$, with zero endpoint change in center-of-mass kinetic energy and separately tracked external-field potential energy, $\Delta U_c[P_s]=Q[P_s]+W_{\rm on}[P_s]$.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[post-td-macroscopic-second-law]]: The total endpoint entropy of the admitted isolated-compound record $\widehat P$ does not decrease.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]: A stable endpoint is an attained global maximum of total entropy on the same exact feasible endpoint set $\mathcal F$.

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[def-td-si-quantities]]: $U_c,Q[P_s],W_{\rm on}[P_s]$ and $p_0V_c$ are in joules; $T_0$ is in kelvins; $S_c$ is in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, so $\Phi_{T_0,p_0}$ is in joules.

steps.text: By [A2] and [F2], $\Delta U_c[P_s]=Q[P_s]-p_0\Delta V_c[P_s]$. By [A1]–[A3], the total entropy change along the isolated-compound extension is $\Delta S_{\rm tot}[\widehat P]=\Delta S_c[P_s]-Q[P_s]/T_0$, because the pressure store has constant entropy. Therefore $$ \Phi_{T_0,p_0}(x_{P_s}^+)-\Phi_{T_0,p_0}(x_{P_s}^-)=\Delta U_c[P_s]+p_0\Delta V_c[P_s]-T_0\Delta S_c[P_s]=Q[P_s]-T_0\Delta S_c[P_s]=-T_0\Delta S_{\rm tot}[\widehat P]\le0 $$ by $T_0>0$ and [F3]. The heat and work are assigned to $P_s$, while their matching reservoir and store changes are assigned to its same-record extension $\widehat P$. [given, A1, A2, A3, F1, F2, F3, F5, algebra]

steps.text: For every $(x,y_R,y_B)\in\mathcal F$, [A2]–[A3] give $E_R(y_R)=E_{\rm tot}-U_c(x)-p_0V_c(x)-C_B$. By [A1], reservoir entropy is affine in this energy, while the pressure-store entropy is constant. This proves the global-minimum conclusion on the precise induced feasible set. [given, A1, A2, A3, F1, F4, algebra] ∎

facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] [[def-td-phase-and-coexistence-domain]]: A generator point is a model-specified state label; the theorem's mixture feasibility is an additional model assumption and does not assert that every phase collection is physically available.

facts.label: A2
facts.text: [A2] [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]: Entropy is a finite state function on the declared physical states. Continuity of $s$ on this compact $K$ is the explicit regularity hypothesis here.

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]] and [[def-probability-measure]]: The Borel sigma algebra is generated by the relatively open subsets of $K$, and each probability measure has total mass one.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] and [[lem-tdmath-measure-integral-agrees-with-root-lebesgue-integral]]: The local nonnegative integral is the supremum of simple-function integrals and agrees with the shared nonnegative Lebesgue integral. Since both signed-integral conventions use the difference of the positive and negative part integrals, they agree on bounded real functions as well.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], and [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]: Bounded Borel real functions are integrable under a finite probability measure; their integrals are linear, order-preserving, and satisfy $|\int f\,dP|\le\int|f|\,dP$.

facts.label: L1
facts.text: [L1] [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]: A continuous real function on a nonempty compact metric space is bounded and attains its minimum and maximum.

facts.label: L2
facts.text: [L2] [[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]], [[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]], and [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: Continuous images of compact metric spaces are compact; compact Euclidean subsets are closed and bounded; closed bounded subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces are compact.

facts.label: L3
facts.text: [L3] [[thm-rank-nullity]]: For a linear map between finite-dimensional vector spaces, domain dimension equals kernel dimension plus image dimension.

If $|f|\le M$ for one such coordinate, [F3] gives $\int_K|f|\,dP\le M P(K)=M$, so $f$ is integrable. [given, A2, F1, F3, L1, L2, construct]

steps.text: Every point of $C$ is a finite convex combination of points $h(x_i)$. If such a representation has $N>d+2$, the linear map $T:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^{d+2}$ defined by $T(c)=(\sum_i c_i h(x_i),\sum_i c_i)$ has a nonzero kernel vector $c$ by [L3], because the coordinate bases give domain dimension $N$ and codomain dimension $d+2$. Thus $\sum_i c_i=0$ and $\sum_i c_i h(x_i)=0$, so $c$ has both positive and negative coordinates. After dropping zero weights from the representation, set $t=\min_{c_i>0}\theta_i/c_i$ and replace each weight $\theta_i$ by $\theta_i-tc_i$. The new weights remain nonnegative, still sum to one, represent the same point, and at least one is zero. Repeating reduces every combination to at most $d+2$ terms. Hence $C$ is the image of $K^{d+2}\times\Delta_{d+2}$ under $\Theta((x_i),(\theta_i))=\sum_{i=1}^{d+2}\theta_i h(x_i)$, where $\Delta_{d+2}:=\{(\theta_i):\theta_i\ge0,\sum_i\theta_i=1\}$; shorter combinations are padded with zero weights and any fixed point of nonempty $K$. Each factor $K$ is closed and bounded by [L2], and $\Delta_{d+2}$ is closed by continuity of the finite coordinate sum and its coordinate inequalities; it is bounded since $0\le\theta_i\le1$. Their product is therefore closed and bounded in $\mathbb R^{(d+1)(d+2)}$, so compact by [L2]. To check $\Theta$ is continuous on this compact parameter set, fix a parameter $((x_i),(\theta_i))$. Each coordinate $h_j$ is bounded by some $M$ on $K$ and is continuous at each of the finitely many $x_i$. For any $\epsilon>0$, choose neighborhoods of the $x_i$ making $|h_j(x_i')-h_j(x_i)|<\epsilon/(2N)$ for every output coordinate $j$, and require $|\theta_i'-\theta_i|<\epsilon/(2N(M+1))$. Since $0\le\theta_i'\le1$ and $|h_j(x_i)|\le M$, each product difference $|\theta_i'h_j(x_i')-\theta_ih_j(x_i)|<\epsilon/N$; summing over $i$ makes each output-coordinate difference smaller than $\epsilon$. Thus $\Theta$ is continuous. The continuous-image clause of [L2] makes its image $C$ compact, and [L2] also makes $C$ closed. [given, L1, L2, L3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

steps.text: Fix any Borel probability $P$ on $K$ and let $y(P):=(\int_K x\,dP,\int_Ks\,dP)=\int_Kh\,dP$, with coordinatewise integration. For $\epsilon>0$, compactness of $H$ gives a finite cover of $H$ by open Euclidean balls of radius $\epsilon$. Their preimages under $h$ are Borel; disjointifying them in a fixed finite order gives a finite Borel partition $(A_i)$ of $K$. For every nonempty part choose $z_i\in A_i$ and put $\theta_i=P(A_i)$. Then $y_\epsilon:=\sum_i\theta_i h(z_i)$ belongs to $C$. For $x\in A_i$, both $h(x)$ and $h(z_i)$ lie in the same radius-$\epsilon$ ball, so each coordinate difference is at most $2\epsilon$. The simple map equal to $h(z_i)$ on $A_i$ has integral $y_\epsilon$ by the simple-integral definition. By linearity and the integral triangle inequality in [F3], each coordinate of $y(P)-y_\epsilon$ has absolute value at most $2\epsilon\sum_iP(A_i)=2\epsilon$. Consequently $\|y(P)-y_\epsilon\|_2\le2\epsilon\sqrt{d+1}$, so the sequence obtained with $\epsilon=1/n$ converges to $y(P)$. Since $C$ is closed by step 2.1, $y(P)\in C$. steps.text: Because $\bar x\in\operatorname{conv}K$, a finite convex combination of generators has barycenter $\bar x$; its corresponding combination of points $h(x)$ shows that $E_{\bar x}:=\{r\in\mathbb R:(\bar x,r)\in C\}$ is nonempty. The set $E_{\bar x}$ is bounded because $C$ is bounded, and it is closed because $C$ is closed and $r\mapsto(\bar x,r)$ is continuous. By [L2] it is compact in $\mathbb R$, so [L1] applied to the identity function yields a maximum $r_*\in E_{\bar x}$. [given, L1, L2, step 2.1, algebra]

steps.text: Represent $(\bar x,r_*)\in C$ by a finite convex combination $\sum_{i=1}^N\theta_i(x_i,s(x_i))$, dropping zero weights. facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] Boundary-chart hypothesis: $\Phi$ is finite and C1 on an open subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^R$ containing $\xi_*$, and its derivative along the affine extent map is the displayed stoichiometric chemical-potential expression throughout $U$. At positive amounts, the expression follows from the local Gibbs differential of [F2]; at zero amounts it is an added model extension.

facts.label: A2
facts.text: [A2] Boundary-inclusive physical model: for the boundary route only, the model declares a state domain containing the zero-amount state at $\xi_*$ and finite C1 maps $\bar U_c,\bar V_c,\bar S_c:U\to\mathbb R$ with units J, $\mathrm{m^3}$, and $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, and $\Phi=\bar U_c+p_0\bar V_c-T_0\bar S_c$. Its isolated compound has an exact feasible set of tuples $(\xi,y_R,y_B)$ whose projection onto extents is $\mathcal F_\nu\cap U$, fixed total energy $\bar U_c(\xi)+E_R(y_R)+E_B(y_B)$, ideal-reservoir entropy $S_R(E_R)=S_{R,0}+E_R/T_0$, constant store entropy, and pressure-store relation $E_B(y_B)-p_0\bar V_c(\xi)=C_B$ throughout that feasible set. The endpoint corresponding to $\xi_*$ is an attained global maximum of the sum of system, reservoir, and store entropies on this exact set. These are explicit additional model premises, not consequences of the positive-mole state domain.

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[pthm-td-fixed-tp-reaction-potential-minimum]]: For an admitted closed process record with the specified ideal reservoir and pressure store, its system potential decreases on every record; an attained global entropy maximum on that exact isolated-compound feasible set gives a global minimum on the projected system state set. For this interior application, that projection contains the system states corresponding to every extent in $\mathcal F_\nu\cap U$. The supplier does not cover zero amounts outside $D_c$.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[pthm-td-potential-differentials]]: On a valid single-phase energy-representation and Gibbs natural-variable chart, $dG=-S\,dT+V\,dp+\sum_j\mu_j\,dn_j$. The identity is used only at positive amounts; at the boundary, [A1] is the separate derivative premise.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[lem-tdmath-stoichiometric-tangent-cone]]: For the nonnegative stoichiometric feasible polyhedron, the tangent cone consists exactly of $h$ with $(\nu h)_j\ge0$ for every active species. At a differentiable local minimum, the directional derivative is nonnegative on that cone; for a differentiable convex objective on a convex domain, this condition is sufficient for a global minimum.

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-probability-measure]], and [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]: Feasible mixtures are countably additive Borel probability measures of total mass one, and their integrals use the stated measure convention.

steps.text:
Since $0<s_0-a\le s(x)<s_0$ on $K$, every feasible $s$ is nonnegative and bounded. For $n\ge2$, put $A_n:=\{x\in K:|x|\ge1/n\}$. Their union is $K$; since $P(K)=1$, countable additivity implies $P(A_n)>0$ for some $n$. On $A_n$, $s\le s_0-a/n^2$, and on its complement $s\le s_0$. For any nonnegative simple function $\varphi\le s$, the measure integral definition [F1] therefore gives
$$
\int_K\varphi\,dP\le(s_0-a/n^2)P(A_n)+s_0P(K\setminus A_n)=s_0-aP(A_n)/n^2<s_0.
$$
Indeed, refine the finitely many level sets of $\varphi$ by $A_n$ and its complement; each simple-function coefficient is bounded by the corresponding pointwise bound on that piece, so the simple-integral formula [F1] gives the inequality. The strict upper bound is independent of $\varphi$, hence its supremum also satisfies $\int_Ks\,dP<s_0$. [given, F1, algebra]

steps.text: For each $0<\epsilon<1$, the measure $P_\epsilon=\tfrac12\delta_{-\epsilon}+\tfrac12\delta_{\epsilon}$ is a Borel probability measure on $K$, has mean zero, and satisfies $\int_Ks\,dP_\epsilon=s_0-a\epsilon^2$. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ shows that the supremum is $s_0$. Step 1.1 shows that no feasible measure attains it. Thus the false statement fails even with a bounded positive continuous concave extension, because the admissible generator set excludes its maximizing barycenter. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[pthm-td-compact-continuous-phase-mixture]]: Under these compactness, continuity, barycenter, and feasibility hypotheses, an entropy-maximizing mixture exists with at most $d+1$ atoms, here $d=1$.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-probability-measure]], and [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]: A Borel probability measure on finite $K$ assigns nonnegative weights summing to one, and the integral of a simple function is the finite weighted sum of its values. The supplier [[pthm-td-compact-continuous-phase-mixture]] defines $\delta_x(A)=1$ when $x\in A$ and $0$ otherwise for Borel $A\subseteq K$.

steps.text: Write $w_0=P(\{0\})$ and $w_1=P(\{1\})$. By [F2], $w_0+w_1=1$ and the barycenter equation is $w_1=\tfrac12$. Hence the only feasible measure is $P_*=\tfrac12\delta_0+\tfrac12\delta_1$. [given, F2, algebra]

Its entropy per mole is the finite simple-function integral
$$
\int_Ks\,dP_*=\tfrac12s(0)+\tfrac12s(1)=\tfrac12s_0+\tfrac12(s_0+a)=s_0+\frac a2.

Since it is the only feasible mixture, it attains the maximum. Its two support points equal $d+1$ for $d=1$, as in [F1]. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

facts.label: A1
facts.text:
[A1] Stability means $U_N\ge-BN$ for every finite configuration and every
$N\ge1$ ([[def-tdmath-stable-power-tempered-particle-model]]).

facts.label: L1
F1
facts.text:
[F1] [[def-countable-choice]] states $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; the standard
Lebesgue measure and box suppliers used here state this assumption explicitly.

facts.label: F2
facts.text:
[F2] [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]] defines
$\lambda_d$ as Lebesgue measure on its measurable sets; restricting it to
Borel sets gives a measure. [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]] gives
$\lambda_d([0,L]^d)=L^d$ under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$;
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]] gives
the rectangle formula for finite products of sigma-finite measures.

facts.label: F3
facts.text:
[F3] [[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]]
ensures the Lebesgue factors are sigma-finite, so the finite product measures
in the Definition exist.

facts.label: F4
facts.text:
[F4] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] defines
$e^x=\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}x^N/N!$, with integer powers as in
[[def-integer-power]]; [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]] proves
convergence for every real $x$.

facts.label: F5
facts.text:
[F5] [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]] gives $e^xe^y=e^{x+y}$, and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]] gives monotonicity of $e^x$.

facts.label: F6
facts.text:
[F6] [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]] defines $0!=1$ and the ordinary
factorial recursion; [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]] defines the series
sum as the supremum of its nonnegative partial sums, allowing $+\infty$.

facts.label: F7
facts.text:
[F7] [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]] identifies
the finite product Borel sigma-algebra, and extended-real measurability means
measurability of preimages of extended-real Borel sets
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Coordinate-difference maps are
continuous, hence Borel under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]]); composition with the Borel
potential preserves measurability
([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]). Finite
sums of the resulting extended-real measurable terms are measurable whenever
defined ([[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]).
On finite energy values $u$, $u\mapsto e^{-\beta u}$ is continuous; assigning
the value $0$ at $u=+\infty$ remains Borel because $\{+\infty\}$ is Borel
([[def-extended-reals]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]). The box indicator is measurable,
so the integrand extended by zero off $\Lambda_L^N$ is product-measurable.

facts.label: F8
facts.text:
[F8] [[lem-integer-part]] gives, for every real $x$, an integer
$\lfloor x\rfloor$ with $\lfloor x\rfloor\le x<\lfloor x\rfloor+1$.

steps.text: By [A1] and $\beta>0$, every configuration satisfies $0\le e^{-\beta U_N}\le e^{\beta BN}$, with the value $0$ when $U_N=+\infty$. Fact [F7] makes the integrand and its restriction to $\Lambda_L^N$ measurable. Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^r c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ be any nonnegative simple minorant of $e^{-\beta U_N}\mathbf1_{\Lambda_L^N}$, written with disjoint measurable sets and finite coefficients $c_j\ge0$ as in [L1]. Outside $\Lambda_L^N$ the minorant is zero, so every $A_j$ with $c_j>0$ is contained in $\Lambda_L^N$; on each such set $c_j\le e^{\beta BN}$. Since [F2] gives a finite measure for the box, each such $A_j$ has finite measure. Countable additivity gives finite additivity on these disjoint sets, while monotonicity follows by decomposing the box into their union and its measurable complement. Consequently $$\int s\,d\lambda_d^{\otimes N}=\sum_{c_j>0}c_j\lambda_d^{\otimes N}(A_j) \le e^{\beta BN}\sum_{c_j>0}\lambda_d^{\otimes N}(A_j) =e^{\beta BN}\lambda_d^{\otimes N}\!\left(\bigcup_{c_j>0}A_j\right) \le e^{\beta BN}\lambda_d^{\otimes N}(\Lambda_L^N).$$ Taking the supremum over these minorants in [L1] proves the same bound for the restricted integrand's nonnegative integral. [A1, F1, F7, L1, algebra]

Therefore $$\sum_{N>n_L}Z_{L,N}\le e^{-KL^d}\sum_{N>n_L}\frac{(eQL^d)^N}{N!}\le e^{-KL^d}e^{eQL^d}=e^{(eQ-K)L^d}\le e^{-L^d}.$$ The second inequality extends a nonnegative partial tail to the full exponential series; the equality uses [F5], and the last inequality follows from $K>eQ+1$ and [F5]. Taking suprema over $M$ in the nonnegative-series definition [F6] gives $\Xi_L=\Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}+\sum_{N>n_L}Z_{L,N}$; subtraction is valid because step 3.1 proves $\Xi_L<\infty$. Since $\Xi_L\ge1$, step 3.2 implies $\Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}\ge\Xi_L-e^{-L^d}\ge(1-e^{-L^d})\Xi_L$. [F6, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

Since $\Xi_L\ge1$, step 3.2 implies $\Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}\ge\Xi_L-e^{-L^d}\ge(1-e^{-L^d})\Xi_L$.

facts.label: F1
facts.text:
[F1] [[def-tdmath-stable-power-tempered-particle-model]] defines $U_N$,
stability, and the power-tail bound: for $\|x\|_2\ge R$, $\phi(x)$ is real
and its real absolute value $|\phi(x)|$ is at most $C\|x\|_2^{-d-\epsilon}$.

facts.label: F2
facts.text:
[F2] [[lem-tdmath-particle-exponential-cutoff]] gives the exact grand
partition definition, $1\le\Xi_L\le e^{QL^d}$, and the particle-cutoff lower
bound, where $Q=ae^{\beta B}$.

facts.label: F3
facts.text:
[F3] [[lem-tdmath-separated-cube-tail-bound]] gives the uniform bound
$D\le(C/2)Mn^2S_{d,\epsilon}g^{-d-\epsilon}$ on all cross-cube energies.

facts.label: F4
facts.text:
[F4] [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] defines the local nonnegative integral as
the supremum over simple minorants; that current batch-11 carrier is a draft
definition with its interface inspected. The local bridge
[[lem-tdmath-measure-integral-agrees-with-root-lebesgue-integral]] proves that
this integral agrees with the shared nonnegative Lebesgue integral. This is the
interface needed to apply the published Tonelli theorem to the partition
integrals.

facts.label: F5
facts.text:
[F5] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] states that for
sigma-finite measure spaces and a nonnegative product-measurable function, the
product integral equals either iterated integral. The Euclidean product Borel
theorem [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]] ensures
the finite-configuration integrand is product-measurable.

facts.label: F6
facts.text:
[F6] [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]
supplies the rectangle formula and uniqueness for the finite product measures;
the Lebesgue factors are sigma-finite by
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]].

facts.label: F7
facts.text:
[F7] [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]
preserves each cube integral under a common translation of its particle
coordinates. The corresponding finite product measure is translation-invariant
by the rectangle formula and uniqueness in [F6].

facts.label: F8
facts.text:
[F8] [[def-countable-choice]] is the exact $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ assumption
used by the Lebesgue-measure suppliers
[[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]] and
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]]. No full
arbitrary-index choice is used in the block construction.

facts.label: F9
facts.text:
[F9] Positive real powers obey the exponent laws and are continuous on positive
bases ([[def-real-power]], [[thm-real-power-laws]],
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]). The natural logarithm is
continuous, strictly increasing and onto $\mathbb R$ on $(0,\infty)$
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]); together with
[[thm-exponential-limits-and-range]], this gives $\ell^\gamma\to0$ for every
$\gamma<0$ and $\ell^\gamma\to\infty$ for every $\gamma>0$.

facts.label: F10
facts.text:
[F10] [[lem-integer-part]] gives an integer $m$ with $m\le x<m+1$ for every
real $x$.

facts.label: F11
facts.text:
[F11] Factorials satisfy $0!=1$ and the recursion
$(N+1)!=(N+1)N!$ ([[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]).

facts.label: A1
facts.text:
[A1] Since $p_L$ is defined for $L\ge1$, write
$$\limsup_{L\to\infty}p_L:=\inf_{T\ge1}\sup_{L\ge T}p_L,\qquad \liminf_{L\to\infty}p_L:=\sup_{T\ge1}\inf_{L\ge T}p_L.$$
These are finite because [F2] bounds $p_L$ in $[0,Q]$.

Set $\alpha:=\frac12\bigl(1+d/(d+\epsilon)\bigr)$ and
$g_\ell:=\ell^\alpha$. Then $d/(d+\epsilon)<\alpha<1$ and
$\ell^d g_\ell^{-d-\epsilon}=\ell^{d-\alpha(d+\epsilon)}\to0$ while
$g_\ell/\ell\to0$. Fix a sufficiently large $\ell\ge1$ so that
$g_\ell\ge R$. For $L\ge\ell+g_\ell$, set
$m_L:=\lfloor L/(\ell+g_\ell)\rfloor$. Since $L/(\ell+g_\ell)\ge1$, [F10]

They lie inside $[0,L]^d$ and have pairwise gaps at least $g_\ell$.

steps.text:
First, if $T$ is a bijection whose map and inverse are measurable and that
preserves measure, meaning $\mu(T^{-1}A)=\mu(A)$ for every measurable $A$,
then $\mu(TA)=\mu(A)$ as well by applying this identity to $TA$; thus $T^{-1}$
also preserves measure. Such a map preserves nonnegative integrals: for an
indicator $\mathbf1_A$,
$\int\mathbf1_A\circ T\,d\mu=\mu(T^{-1}A)=\mu(A)=\int\mathbf1_A\,d\mu$;
finite sums give the same equality for simple functions. If $f\ge0$ is
measurable, composition with $T$ sends every simple minorant of $f$ to a
simple minorant of $f\circ T$ with the same simple integral. Taking the
supremum in [F4] gives $\int f\,d\mu\le\int f\circ T\,d\mu$, and applying
this inequality to $T^{-1}$ and $f\circ T$ gives equality. The same supremum
definition shows monotonicity: $f\le h$ implies $\int f\,d\mu\le\int h\,d\mu$.
For $N\ge1$ identical Lebesgue factors, a coordinate permutation preserves the
finite product measure: the permutation is a Borel isomorphism, so its
push-forward is sigma-finite, and that push-forward agrees with the original
measure on rectangles by the rectangle formula in [F6]; finite-product
uniqueness, obtained by iterating the uniqueness clause in [F6], makes the
measures equal. When $N=0$, there is one empty configuration and one empty
assignment, so the equality is immediate.
Now fix occupancies $0\le N_j\le n_\ell$ with total $N=\sum_jN_j$. The
ordered configurations in the disjoint cubes with exactly these occupancies
are partitioned by assignments of the $N$ particle labels to cubes. The number
of assignments is $N!/(\prod_jN_j!)$: order all $N$ labels, then note that
each assignment occurs exactly $\prod_jN_j!$ times from within-cube reorderings.
Any two such assignments differ by a permutation of the $N$ labels, and the
corresponding coordinate permutation maps one assignment domain to the other.
The potential is even, so $U_N$ is invariant under particle-coordinate
permutations. The integral invariance just proved therefore makes the
assignment-domain integrals equal. [F1, F4, F6, F11, given, step 1.1, algebra]

steps.text:
Restrict the grand partition sum in $[0,L]^d$ to configurations with no
particles outside these cubes and at most $n_\ell$ particles in each cube,
where $n_\ell$ is the cutoff from [F2]. If two cubes have index difference
$k\ne0$, the coordinate gap in a coordinate attaining $\|k\|_\infty$ is at
least $\|k\|_\infty g_\ell$; [F3] therefore bounds the total absolute
inter-cube energy by
$$D_L\le\frac C2M_Ln_\ell^2S_{d,\epsilon}g_\ell^{-d-\epsilon}.$$
Thus $U_N=\sum_jU_{N_j}^{(j)}+U_{\mathrm{cross}}$ with

$k\ne0$, the coordinate gap in a coordinate attaining $\|k\|_\infty$ is at
least $\|k\|_\infty g_\ell$; [F3] therefore bounds the total absolute
inter-cube energy by
$$D_L\le\frac C2M_Ln_\ell^2S_{d,\epsilon}g_\ell^{-d-\epsilon}.$$

On each assignment domain from step 2.1, the pointwise lower bound in

step 2.1 and repeated application of [F5] and the rectangle formula in [F6]
factor the resulting lower bound's integral into the product of the translated
one-cube integrals. For a cube indexed by $j$ with $N_j\ge1$, common
translation by $(\ell+g_\ell)j$ is a Borel isomorphism mapping
$[0,\ell]^{dN_j}$ onto $C_j^{N_j}$ and preserves its finite product measure:
the push-forward is sigma-finite and, on rectangles, this follows from
single-coordinate translation invariance [F7] and the rectangle formula [F6];
uniqueness in [F6] gives equality of the product measures. Pair differences,
hence the within-cube integrand, are
unchanged by this translation, so the integral invariance proved in step 2.1
identifies the integral over $C_j^{N_j}$ with its origin-centered integral over

steps.text:
The integer-part bounds in step 1.1 give
$L/(\ell+g_\ell)-1<m_L\le L/(\ell+g_\ell)$, so
$m_L/L\to(\ell+g_\ell)^{-1}$ and $M_L/L^d\to(\ell+g_\ell)^{-d}$.
By [F2], $\Xi_\ell^{\mathrm{cut}}\ge(1-e^{-\ell^d})\Xi_\ell$, so
$\log\Xi_\ell^{\mathrm{cut}}\ge\ell^dp_\ell+\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})$.
Taking logarithms in step 3.1, dividing by $L^d$, and using step 2.2 gives
$$p_L\ge\frac{M_L}{L^d}\left(\ell^dp_\ell+\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})-\frac{\beta C}{2}n_\ell^2S_{d,\epsilon}g_\ell^{-d-\epsilon}\right).$$
Taking the lower limit and using the volume ratio above yields the same bound
with $M_L/L^d$ replaced by $(\ell+g_\ell)^{-d}$. The cutoff definition [F2]
and $\ell\ge1$ give
$n_\ell\le K\ell^d+1\le(K+1)\ell^d$. Factoring
$(\ell/(\ell+g_\ell))^d$ and using this estimate in the negative error term
therefore gives
$$\liminf_{L\to\infty}p_L\ge\left(\frac{\ell}{\ell+g_\ell}\right)^d\left[p_\ell+\ell^{-d}\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})-\frac{\beta C}{2}(K+1)^2S_{d,\epsilon}\ell^dg_\ell^{-d-\epsilon}\right].$$

As $\ell\to\infty$, the prefactor tends to $1$. Also

Let $\overline p=\limsup_{\ell\to\infty}p_\ell$. By [A1], for every
$\eta>0$ and every $T\ge1$ there is an $\ell\ge T$ with

shows $\liminf p_L\ge\limsup p_L$. [A1, step 5.1, choose, algebra]

steps.text:
For any $S,T\ge1$, choose $L\ge\max(S,T)$. Then
$\inf_{x\ge S}p_x\le p_L\le\sup_{x\ge T}p_x$. Taking the supremum over $S$
and then the infimum over $T$ proves
$\liminf p_L\le\limsup p_L$ by [A1]. Together with step 6.1, the two finite
tail bounds equal a number $p$. For every $\eta>0$, their definitions give
tail thresholds with $\inf_{L\ge T_-}p_L>p-\eta$ and
$\sup_{L\ge T_+}p_L<p+\eta$; hence $|p_L-p|<\eta$ for all sufficiently large
$L$. The limit is finite by [F2]. This proves existence for the specified
free-cube reduced grand pressure. [A1, F2, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

steps.text: For the finite product model of the Statement, the diagonal Gibbs operator satisfies $K_\beta u_{\mathbf n}=e^{-\beta E(\mathbf n)}u_{\mathbf n}=\prod_{r=1}^m q_r^{n_r}u_{\mathbf n}$, where $q_r=e^{-\beta\varepsilon_r}$. For $N\ge1$ let $C_{r,N}=\{0,\ldots,N\}$ for a bosonic factor and $C_{r,N}=\{0,1\}$ for a fermionic factor, and put $C_N=\prod_rC_{r,N}$. These are finite increasing sets whose union is $\mathcal C$. Finite distributivity gives $\sum_{\mathbf n\in C_N}\prod_rq_r^{n_r}=\prod_r\sum_{n_r\in C_{r,N}}q_r^{n_r}$. By the positive-basis trace convention in [F1] and the nonnegative-sum convention [F7], the full trace is the supremum of its finite subsums; every finite subset of $\mathcal C$ is contained in some $C_N$. Hence $0<Z=\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{\mathbf n\in C_N}\prod_rq_r^{n_r}=\prod_{r=1}^m Z_r<\infty$, where $Z_r=Z_B$ or $Z_F$ from steps 1.1–1.2. The canonical basis law is therefore $P(\mathbf n)=\prod_r(q_r^{n_r}/Z_r)$. For fixed factor $s$ and occupation $k\in\mathcal C_s$, summing over the other labels in $C_N$ with $n_s=k$ gives $(q_s^k/Z)\prod_{r\ne s}\sum_{n_r\in C_{r,N}}q_r^{n_r}$ once $N\ge k$; taking $N\to\infty$ and using $Z=\prod_rZ_r$ yields the marginal $P_s(k)=q_s^k/Z_s$. facts.text: [F3] [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-trace-class-operator]], and [[thm-trace-of-a-positive-operator-is-the-sum-of-its-eigenvalues]]: under Countable Choice, a positive trace-class operator has finite trace equal to the sum of its nonnegative eigenvalues with multiplicity.

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]]: the nonnegative countable partition sum is the supremum of its finite subsums, so a finite normalizer bounds the sum over every subset of the listed states.

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[def-td-si-quantities]]: $\varepsilon$ is in joules and $\beta$ in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$, so $\beta\varepsilon$ is dimensionless.

facts.label: F6
facts.text: [F6] [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]] defines $\ell^2(\mathcal F)$ and its inner product. The explicit enumeration identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb C)$, which is complete with a dense finite-support subspace by [[lem-tdmath-diagonal-model-hilbert-and-domain]]. The indicator vectors are orthonormal by the coordinate pairing, and their finite linear span is that dense subspace, so they form an orthonormal basis.

facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] The basis indices are all finite-support occupation sequences with physical energy $E_n=\varepsilon\sum_jn_j$ joules, so their Gibbs eigenvalues are $e^{-\beta E_n}=q^{\sum_jn_j}$; every finite-mode subset is a subset of this full basis.

facts.label: A2
facts.text: [A2] AC and Countable Choice are assumed through the finite-mode Gibbs result and the trace-class definitions/theorems cited above.

steps.text: The trace contribution from states supported on the first $M$ modes is the finite product $Z_M=(1-q)^{-M}$ by [F1]. Since $c=(1-q)^{-1}>1$, $Z_M=c^M$ is unbounded: writing $c=1+r$ with $r>0$, induction gives $(1+r)^M\ge1+Mr$. The unit convention [F5] makes $\beta\varepsilon$ dimensionless. [F1, A1, F5, algebra]

steps.text: If $K_\beta$ were trace class, [F3] would make its positive eigenvalue sum finite and equal to its trace. For each $M$, the configurations with $n_j=0$ for $j>M$ form a subset of the enumerated states [A1]; [F4] therefore makes their finite-mode partition sum $Z_M$ no larger than the full normalizer. [F1] identifies that subset sum as $Z_M$, and step 1.1 makes $Z_M$ unbounded, a contradiction. Hence $K_\beta$ is not trace class and the countable partition sum has no finite value. The preparation condition [F2] fails, so this model has no normalized countable canonical law of the stated form. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] [[post-nrqm-many-body-canonical-equilibrium-ensemble]]: under AC and Countable Choice, a declared self-adjoint semibounded energy generator with a positive finite Gibbs trace is assigned the density $\rho_\beta=e^{-\beta H}/Z$.

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] [[pthm-td-finite-mode-occupation-and-trace-formulas]]: for a finite tensor product of independent fermionic two-level factors with additive total energy, the trace is the product of the one-mode traces $1+q$, and the joint occupation-basis law is the product of the one-mode Gibbs weights.

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[post-nrqm-framework-autonomous-dynamics]] and [[def-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-framework-evolution]]: closed-system evolution is $\rho(t)=U_t\rho_0U_t^*$ with $U_t=e^{-itH/\hbar}$.

facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] Each site has $q=1/2$, and the initial vector is the ground energy eigenvector $|00\rangle$ of $H$.

steps.text: The product trace in [F2] is $Z=(1+q)^2=9/4$. By the Gibbs assignment [F1] and the product-basis energies from the Statement, $P(n_1,n_2)=q^{n_1+n_2}/Z$; at $q=1/2$, the probabilities on $(00,01,10,11)$ are $(4/9,2/9,2/9,1/9)$. In particular, the Gibbs probability of $|11\rangle$ is $1/9>0$. [F1, F2, A1, algebra]

steps.text: Since $H|00\rangle=0$, $U_t|00\rangle=|00\rangle$ for every $t$; thus $\rho(t)=|00\rangle\langle00|$. Its probability for the projector $|11\rangle\langle11|$ is zero at every time, unlike the Gibbs value $1/9$. The state therefore never reaches this Gibbs density under the declared unitary evolution. [F3, A1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] Finite products carry the product sigma-algebra generated by measurable rectangles, and finite products of standard Borel spaces are standard Borel ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-standard-borel-space]], [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]).

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] A pi-system generating a sigma-algebra determines every lambda-system containing it ([[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]]).

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] Use the left-closed, right-open dyadic intervals $I_{m,k}=[k2^{-m},(k+1)2^{-m})$, $0\le k<2^m$. The natural/integer indices and integer powers are those of [[def-natural-numbers]], [[def-integers]], and [[def-integer-power]]; their Borel and partition properties are proved locally below, rather than attributed to a supplier with the opposite face convention.

steps.text: On the component of configurations with exactly $n$ points, $N_B(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{j=1}^n\mathbf1_B(x_j)$ is Borel for every Borel $B\subseteq C$. The count of $C$ identifies the component $n$, so every count map is Borel on the full disjoint union. Thus the count-generated sigma-algebra is contained in the sorted-list Borel sigma-algebra. [F1, algebra]
steps.claim: On the component of configurations with exactly $n$ points, $N_B(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{j=1}^n\mathbf1_B(x_j)$ is Borel for every Borel $B\subseteq C$. The count of $C$ identifies the component $n$, so every count map is Borel on the full disjoint union. Thus the count-generated sigma-algebra is contained in the sorted-list Borel sigma-algebra.

steps.text: Each $I_{m,k}$ is Borel as the intersection of a closed ray and an open ray. Distinct interval interiors are disjoint and an adjacent endpoint belongs only to the interval beginning there. Induction on the number of adjacent intervals gives $\bigcup_{k<j}I_{m,k}=[0,j2^{-m})$; at $j=2^m$ this is $[0,1)$. Thus they partition the reference interval. Each interval is the union of its two intervals at the next level, so the partition refines and its mesh tends to zero. Cartesian products give the corresponding Borel partitions of $C$. [F1, F3, algebra]

Distinct interval interiors are disjoint and an adjacent endpoint belongs only to the interval beginning there. Induction on the number of adjacent intervals gives $\bigcup_{k<j}I_{m,k}=[0,j2^{-m})$; at $j=2^m$ this is $[0,1)$. Thus they partition the reference interval. Each interval is the union of its two intervals at the next level, so the partition refines and its mesh tends to zero. Cartesian products give the corresponding Borel partitions of $C$.

steps.text: Let $(T,\mathcal T)$ be any measurable space. For $H\in\mathcal B(C)\otimes\mathcal T$, define $M_H(\eta,t)=\sum_{x\in\eta}\mathbf1_H(x,t)$. The class of such $H$ for which $M_H$ is measurable with respect to the count sigma-algebra times $\mathcal T$ contains every rectangle $A\times D$, since $M_{A\times D}(\eta,t)=N_A(\eta)\mathbf1_D(t)$. It is closed under relative complements because $M_{(C\times T)\setminus H}=N_C-M_H$, and under disjoint countable unions by pointwise convergence of finite partial sums. Rectangles form a generating pi-system, so [F2] proves measurability for every product-measurable $H$. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

Rectangles form a generating pi-system, so [F2] proves measurability for every product-measurable $H$.

steps.text: Fix a component with $n$ distinct points and an index $k\leq n$. Recover the coordinates of the $k$th lexicographic point recursively. Initially the selected prefix is empty and its rank is $r=k$. At coordinate $j$, with measurable prefix $p=(a_1,\ldots,a_{j-1})$, use step 2.1 on the Borel set $H_j=\{(x,p,t):x_\ell=p_\ell\ (\ell<j),\ x_j<t\}$, where $t\in[0,1]$. For each dyadic interval $I=[u,v)$ in coordinate $j$, the number of points matching the prefix and having $x_j\in I$ is $M_{H_j}(\eta,p,v)-M_{H_j}(\eta,p,u)$, hence is measurable. The interval containing the $r$th such coordinate is the first whose cumulative count reaches $r$; the nested interval closures have diameters tending to zero, so their left endpoints converge to that coordinate $a_j$. The count of matching points with $x_j<a_j$ is $M_{H_j}(\eta,p,a_j)$, measurable by step 2.1 after composition with the measurable prefix and $a_j$. Subtracting it from $r$ gives the positive rank among points with the extended prefix. [F3, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct]

For each dyadic interval $I=[u,v)$ in coordinate $j$, the number of points matching the prefix and having $x_j\in I$ is $M_{H_j}(\eta,p,v)-M_{H_j}(\eta,p,u)$, hence is measurable. The interval containing the $r$th such coordinate is the first whose cumulative count reaches $r$; the nested interval closures have diameters tending to zero, so their left endpoints converge to that coordinate $a_j$. The count of matching points with $x_j<a_j$ is $M_{H_j}(\eta,p,a_j)$, measurable by step 2.1 after composition with the measurable prefix and $a_j$. Subtracting it from $r$ gives the positive rank among points with the extended prefix.

steps.text: The recursive choice in step 3.1 is the usual lexicographic ordering rule: among points with a fixed prefix, sort by the next coordinate, retain the value at the current rank, then subtract the points strictly below it to obtain the rank among ties. After coordinate $d$, distinctness leaves exactly one point, namely $x_k$. Thus all coordinate functions of every sorted point are count-measurable. The Borel sigma-algebra on the sorted-list component is generated by its coordinate maps, so it is contained in the count-generated sigma-algebra there. [step 3.1, F1]

steps.text: The count $N_C$ partitions the full configuration space into its countable components. Applying step 4.1 on each component shows that every sorted-list Borel set is count-measurable; step 1.1 proves the reverse inclusion. The displayed sigma-algebra equality follows. [step 1.1, step 4.1, F1] ∎

facts.label: A1
facts.text: [A1] AC is part of the Poisson reference construction and of its countable product existence ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]).

facts.label: F1
facts.text: [F1] On each unit cell, the count has law $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n/n!$ and, conditional on $n$, the points are independent uniform points subsequently sorted. Finite cell families are independent ([[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]).

facts.label: F2
facts.text: [F2] The number of length-$n$ label sequences with category counts $(n_0,\ldots,n_s)$ is the multinomial coefficient, and its finite expansion is the multinomial theorem ([[def-multinomial-coefficient]], [[thm-multinomial-theorem]]).

facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] Exponentials turn sums into products ([[thm-exponential-addition-formula]]).

facts.label: F4
facts.text: [F4] The configuration sigma-algebra is generated by bounded-Borel count maps, finite count cylinders form a generating pi-system, and agreement there determines probability laws ([[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]], [[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]]).

facts.label: F5
facts.text: [F5] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]: the real exponential is its everywhere convergent factorial power series. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]] permits expectations of increasing nonnegative partial sums and countable sums.

steps.text: Fix one unit cell $C_i$ and a finite Borel partition $B_0,\ldots,B_s$ of it. Put $v_j=|B_j|$, so $\sum_jv_j=1$. Conditional on the cell count $N=n$, the $n$ independent uniform points give category-count probability $n!\prod_jv_j^{n_j}/\prod_jn_j!$ for $\sum_jn_j=n$. Multiplying by the Poisson count probability $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n/n!$ gives $e^{-\lambda}\prod_j(\lambda v_j)^{n_j}/n_j!=\prod_je^{-\lambda v_j}(\lambda v_j)^{n_j}/n_j!$, by [F3]. This factors into the Poisson probabilities of the disjoint cell pieces, including the complement $B_0$; hence their counts are independent Poisson variables with respective means $\lambda v_j$. Zero-volume pieces have count zero almost surely by the same formula. [A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]
steps.claim: Fix one unit cell $C_i$ and a finite Borel partition $B_0,\ldots,B_s$ of it. Put $v_j=|B_j|$, so $\sum_jv_j=1$. Conditional on the cell count $N=n$, the $n$ independent uniform points give category-count probability $n!\prod_jv_j^{n_j}/\prod_jn_j!$ for $\sum_jn_j=n$. Multiplying by the Poisson count probability $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n/n!$ gives $e^{-\lambda}\prod_j(\lambda v_j)^{n_j}/n_j!=\prod_je^{-\lambda v_j}(\lambda v_j)^{n_j}/n_j!$, by [F3]. This factors into the Poisson probabilities of the disjoint cell pieces, including the complement $B_0$; hence their counts are independent Poisson variables with respective means $\lambda v_j$. Zero-volume pieces have count zero almost surely by the same formula.

steps.text: Each bounded $A_j$ intersects only finitely many unit cells. Apply step 1.1 to the partition formed by the sets $A_j\cap C_i$ and their complement in each such cell. Independence within each cell and independence between cell configurations show that all component counts, indexed by both $j$ and $i$, are independent Poisson variables. [A1, step 1.1, F1, construct]
steps.claim: Each bounded $A_j$ intersects only finitely many unit cells. Apply step 1.1 to the partition formed by the sets $A_j\cap C_i$ and their complement in each such cell. Independence within each cell and independence between cell configurations show that all component counts, indexed by both $j$ and $i$, are independent Poisson variables.

steps.text: For fixed $j$, sum the component counts over its finitely many cells. The sum of independent Poisson variables of means $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_q$ has mass at $n$ equal to $e^{-\sum\mu_i}(\sum\mu_i)^n/n!$: expand $(\sum_i\mu_i)^n$ by [F2], then use the product of the component masses. Thus $N_{A_j}$ is Poisson with mean $\lambda\sum_i|A_j\cap C_i|=\lambda|A_j|$. The groups of components for different $j$ are disjoint independent families, so their sums remain independent. [A1, step 2.1, F2, F3, algebra]

The sum of independent Poisson variables of means $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_q$ has mass at $n$ equal to $e^{-\sum\mu_i}(\sum\mu_i)^n/n!$: expand $(\sum_i\mu_i)^n$ by [F2], then use the product of the component masses. Thus $N_{A_j}$ is Poisson with mean $\lambda\sum_i|A_j\cap C_i|=\lambda|A_j|$. The groups of components for different $j$ are disjoint independent families, so their sums remain independent.

steps.text: Put $\theta=\lambda|A|$. The count mass in step 3.1 gives, by nonnegative partial sums and [F5], $$E_{Q_\lambda}e^{aN_A}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}e^{an}e^{-\theta}\frac{\theta^n}{n!}=e^{-\theta}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\theta e^a)^n}{n!}=\exp\!\left(\theta(e^a-1)\right).$$ For $\theta=0$, the count is zero almost surely and both sides are one, so no ambiguous zero power is needed. This establishes the exponential-moment interface before entropy estimates use it. [A1, F3, F5, step 3.1, algebra]

This establishes the exponential-moment interface before entropy estimates use it.

steps.text: Let $A_1,\ldots,A_r$ be pairwise disjoint and, for each $j$, consider a finite count-cylinder event in the restriction to $A_j$. Refine the finitely many counting sets in each event into their disjoint atoms inside $A_j$. Step 3.1 gives independent Poisson counts on all these atoms across every $j$; the event for each restricted configuration is a measurable function only of its own atom counts. Thus finite cylinder events factor across $j$. The restriction sigma-fields are generated by these cylinders, so repeated pi-lambda extension proves independence of the restrictions themselves. [A1, step 3.1, F4]

steps.text: For a finite family of bounded Borel sets $A_1,\ldots,A_s$, partition their union into the finitely many disjoint Boolean atoms formed by the sets and their complements. Every $N_{A_j}$ is a sum of the counts on these atoms. Translation preserves each atom's volume, so step 3.1 gives the same joint distribution of this whole count vector under $Q_\lambda$ and its translate. steps.text: For uniqueness, let $T_1,T_2$ be two solutions in the stated regularity class and set $w=T_1-T_2$. Then $w_t=a\Delta w$, $\partial_nw=0$, and $w(\cdot,0)=0$. At each fixed time, $w$ and its spatial derivatives through order two are continuous on the compact rectangle, so the integrands $w\,\partial_i^2w$ and $|\partial_iw|^2$ are bounded and hence $L^1$ for the finite Lebesgue product measure. Apply [F10] successively in the three coordinate factors to identify the rectangle integrals with the iterated one-dimensional integrals. The product rule and [F8] then give $\int_0^{L_i}w\,\partial_i^2w=[w\partial_iw]_0^{L_i}-\int_0^{L_i}|\partial_iw|^2$. The boundary terms vanish by the homogeneous Neumann condition, so $E'(t)=2a\int_\Omega w\Delta w=-2a\int_\Omega|\nabla w|^2\le0$. Thus $E(0)=0$ and $E(t)\ge0$ imply $E(t)=0$; continuity of $w$ gives $w=0$ everywhere. The formula therefore gives the unique solution in the stated class.
